utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to you, Mr. Jones, as well. Perhaps unnecessary, but I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Waespi will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that the Croatian Army had never executed an offensive campaign prior to the series of operations involving Operation Storm, and that was at pages 2902, lines 23 to 25. Now, were you aware that there was an operation called Flash in early May 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That was an offensive operation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That was an offensive operation.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I talked about when I referred to offensive campaign, I included from Summer 94 through Operation Storm and the continuing campaign through -- to -- Operations Maestral and Southern Move.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But there was also an offensive campaign in 1993 called Operation Medak Pocket; were you aware that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you haven't heard that there were war crimes with which the commander was charged which resulted in convictions. You are haven't heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not my focus for what I was asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you would accept that there were operations of offensive character prior to 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it, but that's for you to, I think, to submit. I don't know. I did not look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but you testified that there were no operations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was none of which I knew of that General Gotovina had led at this magnitude of this level of scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, just to understand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say, "There was none of which I knew of that General Gotovina had led ..." Now was your testimony yesterday about offensive operations under the leadership of General Gotovina; or was it about offensive operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My testimony yesterday covered the leadership of General Gotovina in the offensive campaign which he conducted. However, in my research of what I read, as they built their army since 1991/1992 I did not see any significant offensive campaign which was similar in complexity or magnitude of what they were undertaking at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 19 of your expert report, and this is about the issue of command climate. And you discussed that yesterday already. And you mentioned yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I think we have the binder. I hate to interrupt you, I'm sorry. If we could provide the witness with a hard copy from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And yesterday you testified about the importance of a leader not just writing documents but, for instance, showing presence at decisive places. That's at page 20926. Let me develop this subject a little bit further. Now, let me start with this. How important is discipline in an army, in any armed formation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's extremely important as well as training. Having people know what's right to do and what's wrong you get through training, and it's through that training you teach them how to -- how to operate, how to take care of their buddies and their teammates and how to execute the mission. It's when they don't know what right looks like indiscipline, and when you don't have a trained force is when indiscipline could be a factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what happens if discipline breaks down?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, normally when that happens and you don't have someone to correct it fairly quickly, you don't achieve what you're set out to do and what you are told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that goes to the core of any hierarchy if discipline breaks down. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's -- you see multiple examples in here, you know, how that paramounts down through the command. If you have an element that's not following the orders, to include on the western flank when the people, the units, there did not launch as they were supposed to at the time and get moving, that is a form of indiscipline when they failed to move when they were supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And as I said, you know, if discipline isn't maintained, that is a disaster for any commander who wants to achieve a mission.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends on the scope and level of the indiscipline, you know, if it is an isolated incident, it can be probably corrected and not impact the total mission; but it certainly reflects on the command, and -- and the perception how well the force is, how trained, if it is professional and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So a breach of discipline wouldn't just be a disappointment as you put it yesterday. It's more than a disappointment?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly any time that a commander's orders are not fulfilled, he's disappointed with the execution of his subordinates as he trained them to do. However, it could be -- have other implications to the success or lack of success of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me put a couple of propositions to you about this subject. Do you agree that any commander by force of his personality, leadership, command style, and general behaviour has considerable influence on the morale, sense of direction, and performance of his staff and subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say majority of commanders do. I wouldn't say any commander. There's some commanders that have different -- use different tactics of leadership. But for the most part, a commander does influence his staff and his subordinate commanders, those he has direct contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he does it for good or for evil, whatever his command style is?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hopefully for good. That's what he is charged with and that's his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So some commanders will be known for proper conduct and strict adherence to the rules and regulations of their armed forces and, indeed, laws of armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Generally some units take out -- take up the personality of their commander and their focus on the mission and success and how that is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And other commanders might be known for turning a blind eye to indisciplined behaviour and even crimes?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would hope not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you seen examples of that in your career?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my career? The last time I think I had seen that, the commander was relieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in relation to orders issued by a commander, he has to make sure that he gets information that the subordinates receive these orders and implement them. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes he personally doesn't make sure, he should have a system set up to make sure that the word gets to his subordinate commanders, especially those in his direct line of supervision. And so there should be set up in the training and communications process a way to either verbally give a command and then follow up with a documented written order, but that should then have a system that permeates all the way down to the lowest level. That would be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it is up to the commander to set up that system either, you know, the addressee, his subordinates report back to him or he or his staff proactively get information about the implementation of these orders.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, at the moment, a commander doesn't know what happens with his orders, he ceases to be a commander because can no longer function. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment, a commander does not know what happens with his orders, he ceased to be a commander because he can't function properly anymore.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's a hypothetical. I don't know -- there's ways of checking to see if his orders got to the people. But to say that once his order do not get down to his subordinates doesn't mean he is no longer the commander. Then he has to take another action if he sees nothing is happening to make sure whatever his intent was or his orders does get down to that appropriate section and/or commander he is targeting. But he would still be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And yes, I agree with you, at least de jure. And if subordinate commanders or any addressee of an order realises that he can get away with not complying with an order, that's also the beginning of the end of a commander's authority.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that's what I would call insubordination and failure to follow orders. That would not -- obviously if a commander -- you had a subordinate commander like that, then your trust and confidence of his ability to lead his troops and follow out the missions that you have been given by your country, would be seriously degraded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these principles we just talked about, about giving orders, apply to all range of topics. It's about logistic, it's about personnel issues, and it's about committing war crimes and trying to stop these crimes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, remember, at the operational level you're going to be given a mission, and you're going be given an orientation for the manoeuvre units. You are going to set the properties, and then it's the orders developed from your subordinate commanders has the detail of how to execute that. But, yes, there should be a continuity of what you said was your priorities to be executed down at the lowest level to move -- for logistics, for examples, to the right place at the right time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if a soldier or an officer is not disciplined for having disobeyed orders or having committed crimes, it could well encourage him to continue with his cause of action. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases I would agree with that. You know, there is responsibilities at all levels for people to make sure that the orders are carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, there has been a decision here at the ICTY which you may be familiar with. The Strugar case, which involves the attack, shelling of Dubrovnik. Have you heard about that case?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now the Appeals Chamber held that, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think getting into a particular legal issue is a matter that should be addressed to the Court. If there is a particular aspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's wait what the question is and then see whether we are seeking legal opinion from this witness or not, and then if you do so, Mr. Waespi, then, of course, we would have to address the matter, whether this witness is a legal expert, yes or not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think it is more a factual observation by the Court, but let's see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The quote is: "A superior's failure to punish a crime of which he has actual knowledge is likely to be understood, at least as acceptance if not encouragement of such conduct with the effect of increasing the risk of new crimes being committed." In line of what you responded to my earlier question, would you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what you're stating, if a commander knows that a crime has been committed, and that he is taken actions to make sure that it is investigated and, no kidding, there's a crime here. He needs to take action of some sort. You know, I go back to you never walk by a mistake so just by -- that's a way of instilling the discipline within your unit, your organisation. If it comes within your scope to do that or to tell someone to do that, then you should take some action to make sure that it is not condoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how important is timing in this respect, if an order is issued and it's not being followed of -- or if undisciplined acts occur, how important is timing in relation to the response by the commander in addressing this failure?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's relevant. It would have to be with a seriousness of the -- of whatever incidents happened, first of all; and then second of all, how that relates to what the commander's focus was at the time. If, in fact, there was something that happened and he became aware of it, he started the process for someone to investigate it, he moves on to focus on his mission at hand because he is in the fight or he is in, in this case, the offensive operation, he's got to weigh that response to that incident as well as protecting the lives of his soldiers and making sure they're focussed on the mission and the fight. So you have to weigh that, but you should come back to it at some point in time and say, Okay what happened? I told you to fix it. Did you fix it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I apologise for interrupting. Page 2, line 2, a reference is to pages 2902. That cannot be correct for yesterday's transcript. Do you have the full page number for me? We are in the 20.000s, so therefore ... is it 20902 or is it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is 20911 at lines 21, 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a question to clarify. If the operational situation allows a commander to address disciplinary issues, you would agree with me that it's important that indisciplined behaviour needs to be addressed immediately; otherwise, you know, it sends out the message: He doesn't really care. He might come back to me in a few days or later. So if the situation allows a commander to address it immediately, he has to do it immediately.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's in the scope of his responsibility and authority, he should do something with it. If he has time to do that and if it's at his level of execution. For example, if something happened and he was made aware of it through the reports, he would make sure that whoever is responsible for oversight of that either call him and tell him and ask him what they did about it. If he had time to do it. If it was his direct responsibility and it was immediate in direct reports then he should deal with it, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You have seen the video with General Gotovina, I understand, prior to testifying. This is the 6th of August video which we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now do you agree with me that he is a very strong commander who leaves clear foot prints about the command climate he wants to impress upon his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you saw in that particular case, and I don't know what he had done in his pattern and how he commanded in the past or spoke with his subordinates, but he certainly had to get their attention during that meeting, because he probably sensed that a -- they were becoming complacent, they had thought they had reached the culminating point, and really they had another fight, and as I testified yesterday, they were very vulnerable at that point in time. I think he was also not only in the -- speaking of Knin, he was concerned --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, let me just go back to my question.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just looking at the video, and I think you observed, as you testified yesterday, the body language of the other --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- people. What kind of a commander was General Gotovina as it came out during his address to his subordinate commanders? Just describe what you have seen: A weak commander, a strong commander, somebody people would listen to or not listen to. Just give us your appreciation.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you would say he was in charge. I would think you would say he was passionate about the mission and the role that he expected of his commanders. He outwardly talked about the lack of performance of the subordinate leader and what his expectations were. And so at that point in time, he was telling his commanders they were not living up to his expectations as professionals. He subsequently then went to the next video which talked about the next mission. So I think that was a way a commander, the one who is in charge, reinforces that he is in charge and gets the subordinate commanders their heads back into the -- focussed on the mission and then leads them, as a teaching point, back into what he expected them to do next. That in itself was a form of disciplining his subordinates, telling them they are not executing to his expectations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move to somewhat related but very important topic in your report and, in fact, in this case. Paragraph 21 of your report says that: "During offensive operations, the commander is focussed towards the front and the main effort. For the HV operating on their own national territory, the responsibilities for the rear area of operations were shared by the regular government, law enforcement forces, and local authorities." And then last sentence of this paragraph: "As a result, it was not up to the HV operational commanders to regulate the transition of responsibility for law and order in the rear area." Now, General, you used the term "rear area" a number of times, many times in this report. Can you define what you mean by that? In general but also specifically which territory it compasses and perhaps we could prepare a series of maps you looked at yesterday, which is D728 on electronic page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think he looked at this map yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So please tell the Trial Chamber how you define rear area.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the rear area is the area behind the -- the combat forces and their immediate subordinate forces, their immediate trained [indiscernible] so they move through an area. So in that case they would encompass, say, for a brigade, in the advance, his rear area may be up to six to ten kilometres, based on how his -- his re-enforcing and artillery were moving through the area with him. Behind that, there would be a rear area which would be subordinated to another command for -- for greater general support of logistics. That is -- that -- that line then is defined generally on boundaries through military graphics of what the boundaries would phase -- would move by phase as you move forward. Now, in this particular case, I noted the order showed and the responsibility showed that the military police would -- would follow the offence and take responsibility immediately as the military forces moved through. To me it didn't delineate what that line was or how close they would follow, so it is kind of hard to determine where the rear area actually began. I would say -- I would assume it began when the military police got into the area, and in a lot of cases as they bypass different cities, they would follow the military and then probably within that area take charge of that city or that community of which was obviously Croatian territory and re-established the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you just said, and this is on page 13, line [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I like the French language, but it comes as a surprise on the English channel. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You talked about his rear area. This is the operational commander's rear area, I take it.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, within each -- each unit would have a rear area. The 4th would have, the 7th would have a trailing area. The logistics for each of those brigade would have a possibility of a rear area but then the larger operations group, when you had four operations group at one point in time and went to three, they would have a rear area of which those subordinate folks -- subordinate commands would then be responsible until the military police moved up through that area and then once those -- once you came to the culminating point of the intermediate objectives, you would turn that area over for specifically re-establishing the rule of law in those areas. You still would have trains and logistics movements through those areas to support your front, offensive forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So in line of what you just said, approximately looking at the map in front of you on the screen, and can you take a pen actually to mark it if you feel comfortable. What's the rear area of General Gotovina's forces that were operating in -- in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, okay. This is on the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this point in time, you had your four groups. It would be hard for me to mark, to define rear area. However, it would be something closer to where the -- the units are than what that dotted line would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. There are a couple of -- a number of lines already, so I'm not sure whether you're marking something ...

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not. It's got positions for the Storm. Positions ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just approximately, if you can. I don't want to force you. But if you can approximately define, with a circle or whatever structure you want to use, what you think is on the 8th August, 1995, the rear area of the forces under the command of General Gotovina. And ...

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously ... I would say it would be something like this. Until such time the military police move up and assume control of the former areas, recognised areas of the country of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you put within this circle, almost, the letter A, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter A?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Just to identify that we all know which is your marking as opposed to all the other markings. You can pick another letter if you feel more comfortable.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put a letter A. Is that what you wanted? Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thanks. Now, can you tell me what the rear area was on the 5th -- on the 6th of August? Was it different or was it approximately the same?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would have to be at the -- at the 6th, it would have to be -- whether 4th or 6th, you know, depending on if it was mobile area, would probably on the 6th be something like this, and on the 4th be something like this. So that line in that rear area would advance as the responsibilities were assumed by the military police and the civilian authorities following closely the offensive forces. And that's just a line on the map. I'm not sure exactly where that was portrayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The second line -- can you mark that with letter B; and the third one with letter C.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, again, just for the sake of the record, the letter B would be the rear area on which date?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said the 6th, and probably C would be where the rear area was on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, if this --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I would imagine, as I look at it, these lines would probably come more over this way. You know, as it tapers over towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, it probably wouldn't go down as far there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to have this document admitted into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But before we decide on that, I have some difficulties in clearly defining what has been marked. For letter A, there is a red marking which consists of a line between Obrovac and Grahovo, from Grahovo in south-easterly direction; from Obrovac, also in south-easterly direction, although more to the east, the lines meeting just under where, on the map we find FCP Sajkovici. That's for the 8th. For the 6th, line B, although slightly corrected, is a line correcting Benkovac to Drnis and then further in south-easterly direction; or line C, we find a line, starting between Benkovac and Biograd, going also in south-easterly direction. I am describing the lines, because they're not that clear on our screens at this moment. Mr. Registrar, this marked map would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2617.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit P2617 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, General, were you aware or made aware that there were substantial Split Military District forces staying behind and operating in the Knin area at the end of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by sufficient forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Substantial forces.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Substantial forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Units --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logistics units. Were these not part of the military police. I think when -- on the evening of the 6th when the designated commander of the rear area came in, he assumed responsibility for that area at 1700 on the evening of the 6th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was that commander that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was Mr. Sernak [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was his role?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: His role was to take responsibility and to re-establish the civil authority in the rear area. So at that point in time, that's why I adjusted that other line at 1700 on the 6th August, he came in and assumed responsibility of Knin and the forces thereof. Now there could be other forces in there doing -- as we went into the defence in that area doing some rest as they got ready and/or the following -- preparing for the counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what's the basis for your testimony that General Cermak came and assumed responsibility of Knin and the forces thereof?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in the comments made, even in the video, that General Gotovina said that at -- effective that day, that at 1700, 1730, he was going to arrive and assume control. So I assumed by that that he had -- by his presence, was there to take control of that sector. Now, that, I think, would be -- with the significance of Knin putting leadership at a point of which you have to show control, and somebody in charge of that would be a good thing. It also allowed General Gotovina to focus back forward again and then turn that area back over to the military police and the civilian police and whatever support they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just a very quick word on military police. This -- you know what the correct denomination of that unit was? How was it called?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police unit, the number of the unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, not off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you heard of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it in the task organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And to which unit did it belong?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originally I think it belonged to General Gotovina, his task organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why do you say originally did that change over time?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in his original task organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did that change over time that he lost control over it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appeared to me that at subsequent -- in the meeting with the ministers, it said that the military police and civilian police would then work for -- under the minister of interior and subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see any documents later during August that would indicate that General Gotovina was no --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No longer had control over the military police. The only documents I saw was the fact that related to the military police being subordinated to the minister of the interior. I did not see a further task organisation that General Gotovina had that included the military police. So the absence of that meant they were probably working for somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember the order for active defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, apparently you're moving to another subject. You started your question about the presence of Split Military District forces staying behind, and then the witness answered by asking you what you meant by substantial forces. Then the witness continued to say that responsibility for that area was taken over and, as he told us, under the command of General Cermak. We started with forces. Then we moved to command over those forces. Could you tell us approximately the forces General Cermak had under his command when he took over responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- I could not list them for you. Obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you to list them but to say how much approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that he had the military police and the civilian police that would move through the area that were following the operation. My estimate that would be three to 500 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they were under the command much General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They should have, as they -- and -- and the responsibility was transferred to him. They should have came under his -- his leadership and his authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I used the word command. Apparently you are hesitant to use that same word. Leadership, authority, which is not very much a military --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should have came under his command and control. I did not see him designate other than being a -- a colonel-general what forces were designated to him for command and control. I saw him given responsibilities and authority for the area and being subordinate to civilian police and military police operating and to re-establish the communities and -- and the police stations and so forth, but I did not see his -- his exact task organisation for command and control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there are quite a lot of tasks you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which are, to some extent, of a civilian nature. At least that's how I understand them; whereas, another element seems to of a military nature. Could you tell us what -- how do we have to understand the task of General Cermak? Was he -- was he a military man? Was he in command over troops, although, as you said, perhaps of a limited number of 3 to 500? Could you explain a bit more about what your understanding was of his role.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding was, as I read the documents, that he was -- he was -- had specific responsibility for re-establishing security and the rule of law, the police authority within the rural areas; also designated the court structure and re-establishing what was in the former area of Croatia, the normalcy of the Croatian constitution, whether it be court, laws, police stations and so forth. So his perspective, or my perspective, of his responsibilities was to re-establish that structure within the Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Setting up the court system, would that include civilian courts and military courts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would only be civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only be civil courts. Do you have any -- found any example of how General Cermak was establishing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How he was going executed that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How he did execute that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where specifically did you find his responsibility for setting up the court system.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if you go back to original documents we talked about yesterday, it talked about -- and I said court systems. It is re-establishing the constitution -- constitutional authority over the liberated Croatian territory. So to me, that meant rule of law, court systems, legal authorities, police, and all those things which comprise the normal situation within a community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would then include the whole administrative system as well because you're talking about constitutional -- constitutional authority which includes everything you find in the constitution, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is municipal government, everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, re-establishing the hierarchy within a community of a -- you know, the mayors, the chief of police, those kind of things which you need to also secure the area and/or to execute and -- civil authority over those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, he held a military rank. Could you tell us how the military authority would enable him to -- well, as you tell us, more or less take over responsibility for re-establishment of the whole constitutional order; whereas, normally a military person is limited in his authority. Could you explain to us how that worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to be truthful, Your Honour, I'm not sure why he was given the position of colonel-general, unless President Tudjman saw that he needed that level of authority in recognition amongst his peers to operate in or amongst the total Croatian sector as he was working together with other military commanders. So that would have given him a level, comparable level of authority, as he moved through that area as he re-established the civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what his official position was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know his title right off the top of my head. I would have to look it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you do that during the next break so that we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that we know what you find about this in the papers. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me tidy up the issue of the military police. Let's go back to a document you have seen yesterday, I believe. D281.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be pulled up. That's the order for active defence dated 9th of August, 1995, by General Gotovina. Now, if we go to -- I think it's English page 10 on paragraph 5.11. And perhaps if Mr. Kehoe could assist me what tab number that is in the witness's binder. D218.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, here, we see on page 10, General -- but take your time to sift through it. It's paragraph 5.11. You see in paragraph 5, he gives all kinds of orders to his subordinate units, including the Croatian Guards or 5.9 that is the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade. And then 5.11 he talks about the 72nd Military Police Battalion "that shall protect and monitor the territory, and shall be responsible for any other military and police tasks [sic] at hand." And on the last page, you see that this order --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I was noted something by my colleague about the reading of that. It notes that the 72nd Military Police Battalion along with the MUP bodies. That was left out by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that is my omission; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you go to the last page of this document you see that the 72nd Military Police Battalion was also among the recipients of this order. Now, does that indicate to you that, on the 9th of August, 1995, the military police battalion was still a general asset that could be ordered by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be right with you, counsellor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just take your time.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. And your -- I get what you said. So you're telling me that -- your question is could the military police be ordered by -- by General Gotovina to do things?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The issue -- the reason I brought this document up is because you said that at one time General Gotovina might have lost command --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- over his genuine military police, and my question here is: At this point in time, 9th of August, 1995, is he still in charge of his own military police or has he lost that ability? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears by this -- I don't know if they were still attached or detached with the effective date, but he could still provide them direction. And he did so in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me move back and we can -- you can return this document. Let me move back to my original issue of the -- as I call them substantial forces that were operating in the rear, whatever --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- that's defined of the Split Military District. And I wanted to ask you now specifically were you aware that the Split Military District had, by order in this document that you just looked at, his forward command post in Knin. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware that the Split Military District moved a forward command post into Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Wouldn't that be an important piece of information for you to know when assessing the roles and the responsibility, presence of leadership as you indicated yesterday how important that was, wouldn't that be a key issue for you to know where the forward command post of the commander is?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on who manned this command post. I would -- I find it interesting to find that a Military District command post versus an operational command post would be forward. If, in fact, this command post was going to be utilised by General Cermak, well, then it makes sense. If it was going to be used by General Gotovina, I would say that probably does not make sense and that's where I think he kept his command post over in Bosnia-Herzegovina and then moved forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Looking at the first page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could I ask one clarifying question. You gave two options; that is, it be used by General Gotovina, or being used by General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were these the realistic and the only realistic options you would consider under the circumstances and in view of your knowledge of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if you think about it, the former Split Military District is also back where they tried to establish the non-commissioned officer academy. It was at district headquarters. It had the standard communications probably necessary to run a community and/or peacetime operation. An operational command headquarters, which had to be very mobile, had to be certainly protected and be able to move forward and command its other elements is not as fixed-based. So to move forward elements of the Split district out of Split, the communications and so forth, to support General Cermak would make sense. But for General Gotovina, I would think he would find -- he would have a command post much more mobile, much more focussed forward. So I'm a little confused by moving the Split district up there, and I did not -- I apologise, but I did not research the movement of command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, maybe I should have interspersed with this earlier as opposed to the article "the forward command post," as to the article "a forward command post."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can deal with that in -- Mr. Waespi, at the same time, of course, it would be if you put something to the witness if do you that as specific as possible, so that including the source of the information to the extent possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's a document we have in front of us. That's D281, which is -- is issued from the Knin command post by General Gotovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, the documents are replete in this case, and I'm sure that the Prosecution is not going to debate this that there were multiple forward command post at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss what happened in the presence of the witness. Mr. Waespi, under those circumstances, it would have been appropriate to draw attention of the witness to the fact what the heading of this order was and to ask him how he would consider that. Then he could have told us what he knew about it. But, apparently, and to that extent, he wasn't aware of the forward command post being there at that moment. But that would also, perhaps, have been clue to who was actually using the heading forward command post in a command position. You understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said it could have been used by General Gotovina, could have been used by General Cermak. But it seems that the confusion becomes almost complete. Let's move on and see whether we can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may help clarify that. If you look back at -- on page 16, it talks about the logistic base branch of establishing Knin with the following elements. So obviously this was also a logistic base he was establishing and had to have some forward supervision of those logistics elements. So that to me that would make sense to get a command base in Knin to support the logistics hub that he was creating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And earlier you said, could have been used by General Cermak or by General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was General Cermak in any way involved in logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in support of the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So where you were talking about the forward command post used by General Cermak, that would then exclude for the logistical aspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would probably be mutually supportive of which he could use the communications to talk to his civil police and/or his people in different communities and perform a hub of which he could then direct and monitor their success or -- or their progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just -- with regard to this document, and I'm sure counsel would agree with me, if we can turn to the first page of this document which is the cover page, it clearly shows that it is, in fact, Sajkovici the name and the date of Sajkovici which is, of course, the forward command post that we have talked about routinely in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, of course, is or is not is still established. Let's not discuss in the presence of the witness what it is. First of all, it could have dealt with the matter in re-examination. Apart from that, if there was any matter you could have agree on with Mr. Waespi, then I would expect you to seek such agreement not in the presence of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's stick on -- on this issue and actually the document which is in tab 15, the one you're looking at. Please go to page 4 in the English, paragraph 2, the last sentence in -- on this page. And in B/C/S should be around page 2 or 3. Now, it says here, and this is obviously an order for active defence by General Gotovina: "Split Military District forward command post shall be in Knin." Now, does it indicate to you whether there are any other forward command posts or is it just one, in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the other command post or obviously the operational groups -- and I'm not sure that -- I don't know the transition with General Knin -- or General Gotovina has moved his command post which was in Bosnia-Herzegovina over to Knin or he has retained it where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Were you also aware that there were several reserve battalions that were stationed in Knin from early September onwards? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were several conscript organisations which were logistic-oriented and move forward, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, let's then go back to this document and look on page 9. In English paragraph 5.4, it talks about the 4th Guards Brigade. And then that it shall be withdrawn from the front line. And then in the middle of that paragraph it says: "The reserve battalion shall be stationed in the Knin Barracks," and gives some basic tasks. So that's the 4th Guards Brigade, no logistics units. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the reserve of the 4th Guards Brigade, not a reserve units per se, as I read there. So the 4th Guards Brigade probably kept a battalion in reserve to support their fight and that's the reserve telling them to go to the barracks to get rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct. They are staying in Knin.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's not the logistics units, because --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- you said earlier --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I think concurrently there is logistics units moving forward because Knin has been established as a logistics hub to support the fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. That was my next question. The 40th Engineering Battalion command post was also in Knin. Do you agree with me? This is paragraph 9.1.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes, there were engineers up there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And going back to something you said yesterday. General Gotovina, of course, had to watch his rear, because, as you pointed out he was vulnerable there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it's -- it's an issue of securing your back, he had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I was referring to was when he made it an envelopment move and attacked Knin from the north-east. He has exposed flank on right side which would have been the northern side. Certainly this whole area was probably heavily laden with mines and other things, and that's another reason why you would move the engineer battalion forward. So not particularly the rear area watching your back but your flanks and the area from which the enemy is, you had to be concerned with whether, you know, when he turned, that expose would be to his rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that for all these units and any other Military District of Split units, irrespective of whether they were participating in offences at the front, or whether there were reserve units in -- in the back, or resting, or whatever, for all these units, the commander of the Military District bears ultimate responsibility. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- he bears responsibility for those units that -- in his previous hat, which he was charged and then those which were assigned to him in a task organisation. It goes back to my statement: A commander is responsible for -- for everything which is in his area of operations and then that direct responsibility is sub-organised based on subordinate commanders. So he has a responsibility up until such time he -- he frees that area and turns it over to General Cermak and the others to re-establish Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks for your answer. And just so I understand you, and I'm not that much talking about territory. I'm talking about units or members.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: General Gotovina retains command and responsibility over all the units and members of these units that are attached to the Military District at any given time, whether they are fighting offences or staying in the back being reserve or resting or whatever. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have some responsibility of those units, yes, that are assigned to the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what do you mean by some responsible?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, when you talk about those in the Military District, they have to be assigned to him, and then by virtue of being assigned to the Military District, then he has the authority over the units, command and control and so forth. As you mobilise some of the conscript units for different purposes that may be in the Military District, he may or may not have control over those. They may be assigned to somebody else. So those of which he had assigned to him, he should have responsible and oversight for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on to a different subject, although they are all kind of related. Paragraph 22 in your report. It says: "Also critical for the commander is where he places himself on the battlefield. Normally this is a well-forward command post to ensure that he remains in communications with lead elements. When the commander is well-forward in the battlefield, he must trust that his subordinate leaders are executing their responsibilities as planned and as designated in the written orders process." And you talked about this trust that has to develop between the commander and the subordinates yesterday. Now, you seem to place a lot of emphasise on the written process of commanders, obviously higher echelon commanders. But as we talked about earlier this morning, at the end it's the commander's duty to ensure that these written orders are implemented? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And despite his trust in his subordinates, if a commander has knowledge that his orders aren't implemented, that his trust, you know, is not justified, he has to take action.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, counsellor, of course, you're talking about commanders at all levels?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I think that is also my main point.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Paragraph 26, and I quote: "The source of personnel that comprise units may impact at the level of discipline a unit -- in a unit in an unstructured environment if soldiers have not had the level of training and been subject to the discipline that is required in a very uncertain environment, then the potential for undisciplined behaviour is increased." Now, you mentioned yesterday at page 20907, lines 17 to 19, that General Gotovina knew that he had elements that he could count on but also elements he could not count on. So what's a commander's duty under these circumstances? He has to pay specific attention to these units of whom he knows that they have a problem with discipline. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has to be very careful of the mission he assigns those units. And what I was referring to back in this paragraph, he had units that were formed very rapidly and not afforded the opportunity to establish within their chain of command the training, the authority to discipline, the training to show them what right looks like, and to instill in them what a military organisation, professional military organisation, should act like. He that mix of units. He also had some of his units at which he had been able to spend more time with, and obviously through the offensive campaign, to be able see firsthand their compatibilities. So when have you have that as an operational commander, you must weigh with that with who can -- you think -- are -- have achieved the level of readiness to execute the mission you're going to give them. And, therefore, the care you use is by assigning them, in some cases, a limited objective which would be very -- or more simpler, that they may be able to achieve versus something to be more complex and something which would require more physical stamina and/or a better prepared unit to execute, such as going through the minefields and further achieving the objective. So that is where you weigh that as the operational commander and where you give guidance and priorities to who is in charge of those subordinate units and how you task organise them and make sure there is oversight down to the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But it's not just the operational requirement --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- of putting them on the right task, in terms of your overall objective. An easy task for an undisciplined unit, key task for disciplined unit. It's not just that. It's also the commander has to watch undisciplined units, if he has knowledge about that, very carefully, so that they don't become undisciplined again in the future. And I'm talking about committing crimes. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree -- I mean, no doubt you can't let undisciplined behaviour continue. Now, you need to do something about it. However, you know, as I looked at this very -- what I would say immature professional army, he didn't have a lot of sources of putting people in charge of these units. As you assimilated different units and gave them a title and a mission, that's no way to create an army without training them and showing them what was right. So -- what I saw in a lot of the indisciplined behaviour which happened when you did not have the strength of good supervision in those units probably not totally unpredictable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But the main issue is: If a commander recognises there is a problem, he has to address it and he has to address it in an effective manner.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he must address it in the effected level -- level of effectiveness obviously must play out. He may have to re-address it, if, in fact, it continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, let me try to get -- it's -- it's -- the questions are much in an abstract, on an abstract level. What, Mr. Jones, I think, Mr. Waespi, would like to hear is that if you know that some units of have a reputation or are found to be inclined to undisciplinary and even criminal conduct, would you use those units in a normal way or would you pay specific attention on what tasks you would assign to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously, Your Honour, the latter part, I would -- I'd -- based on the compatibility and the type of unit, I would pay particular attention to what I assigned them to do, and then I would also play close attention on who I put in charge of the units to execute my intent, to make sure they had adequate supervision of qualified leaders, to be able to ensure that, one, something -- undisciplined behaviour does not continue; but, secondly, that they can executed the mission I gave them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now did you come across in your research any such situation where units, perhaps in earlier operations, had shown unruly behaviour or members of those units showing unruly behaviour and that specific action was taken; or are we just talking in the abstract, what if -- I mean, did you find any such thing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in the documentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have been sitting here waiting for the counsel to ask me about the 4th and the 7th because I know those were discussed yesterday, the incidents of Grahovo and so forth and prior to Operation Storm, so why did General Gotovina continue to use them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I thought that was the point we were getting at. Well, obviously he only had some number of forces of which he knew could executed the offensive mission. And those were obviously part of the 4th and 7th and [indiscernible] Battalion. That was at a critical point in time, and moving to the winter of 1994 to position those units was absolutely critical and to replace them in the line would have been probably a very risky manoeuvre. So as you look that in the string of events starting about 30 July all the way up through 8th or 9th of August, he started reiterating the importance of discipline and he also relieved the OG North commander to reinforce the point that he expected discipline in his ranks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we discussed this yesterday, whether the replacement of the -- commander replacement where --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- General Ademi was -- you consider that as a response to apparently unruly behaviour and that's one --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would think, sir, there is probably war-related things that were not evident. Obviously some of the things that happened in Grahovo, and the defence minister noting that there was houses and looting and so forth and him walking into Knin probably did not help his opinion of his OG North commander. So there was a series of events which obviously led him to relieve that commander, because he was not effective with his subordinate commanders in ensuring that their focus of the mission and discipline. You know, also the thing he did was restrict movement, involuntary movement, of the forces to get them away and out of the town so that the police could execute their security mission and re-establish the rule of law. It appeared to me in his sector and these other units, he had -- I would call it indiscipline, but he had people in these other units moving throughout in their own vehicles or somebody else's vehicles during the day, and he restricted movement with the units, that could have helped significantly the others to do their job in the rear, and I thought that was a pretty good thing to do. If you keep units together, you restrict their movement and you keep them focussed on the mission you gave them, then you have a better chance of controlling them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we are back at a concrete level again. I now understand how you -- how you interpret these -- this documentary evidence. Part of your answer was that, apart from paying attention to adequate supervision by qualified leaders; the other one was what tasks to be assigned. Could you give us - apart from that, they should not move around freely - any specific information about perhaps limits or special attention paid to the tasks that would be assigned to units which were known for prior unruly behaviour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think would you see, first of all, in the scheme and knew of the big plan, of which obviously Operation Storm was objective in that plan. He knew that the units on his left flank, or his south-western flank, did not have sufficient training and probably did not have the discipline. I know we used the word "discipline" very loosely here, but in my perspective as a military person they were not ready to prosecute the fight, because they didn't have the training and they probably didn't have the control of their fires, they did not have the leadership down through the non-commissioned officer corps to really kick off, cross the line, and -- and, you know, in a controlled manner on the axis of advance that he wanted to. So he gave them what we call an economy of force mission, which had limited objectives. They want to do an advance to show the enemy forces that they were also attacking, they were attack -- so they could have been perceived of as an attack against all fronts. However, he probably knew because of the composition of that unit they were not capable of achieving a larger objective. So it was also during the course of events, I believe, that he -- he displaced -- as I talk about being at a point on the battlefield where it makes a difference, he flew back there because, after Knin had fell, he saw that the movement of that line was not making any progress, and he went back there and talked to those commanders about picking up and executing the mission. So that, in itself, is where he took risk, he saw the risk, and then he had to go and do something about it, even though those units were not probably very capable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said that he saw that the movement of that line was not making progress and went back and talked to those commanders. Could tell us when did he talk to those commanders? Where did he talk to those commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he flew back on the -- if I remember, somewhere about the 5th. You know, he was delayed going into Knin. During that period, he displaced and went over there because his assessment, not only of Knin as he looked at the total battlefield, was how is the movement of my other units working. And if they did not move then, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- I was asking you where and when he met.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The subject of the discussion, where do we find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- where did I read that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you take your time in the -- during the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would have to find it and go back. I don't have the documents with me. But he left and flew back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was where you found documented [Overlapping speakers] ... of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can find it or if you have any recollection, I'd like to know. Mr. Waespi. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you wish, Mr. President, outside the presence of the witness, we can give you a citation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I have to combine all the information and to verify where it comes from. Mr. Waespi, then I take it, Mr. Misetic, that you would assist Mr. Waespi as well, to trace that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can go through that and show exactly where it is, judge. Well, we'll talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we're close to 10.30. I don't know whether you want to -- we have to some questions to fill the next two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it appropriate moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To take a break. Could you let me first -- we'll have a break, Mr. Jones, and I will ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom. We will resume at approximately five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I take this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see, the witness asked whether he could take something. What would you like to take, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would you like to take with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me to find the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- position and title of General Cermak. I don't have anything with me to look that up unless I take the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you take the book, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could you give us an indication as to how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I hope to finish within next session but perhaps it spills a little bit over into the next one, the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I already inquire whether some of the questions would trigger any need to further ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will now have re-examination for this witness, at least half an hour, I would estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In order to make matters clear, and Mr. Cayley, some of the questions I put to the witness were not primarily aiming at seeking additional information about matters which we have gone over for quite some time. But that I was also intending to see what knowledge the witness had on certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I fully understand what you're saying to me, Your Honour. But I do feel I have an obligation to go back in on some matters, and I'm obviously well aware you don't wanted me re-educating the witness before he goes home, but I really do need to find the basis for some of his conclusions because, like you, I think perhaps there may be a problem there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer I take it that you have understood what, more or less, is of concern and what is not of any concern at this moment. We will have a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises to the parties and to you, Mr. Jones, as well, for the late start. We had an urgent matter to deal with. That's the reason why we have this late start. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: General, let me briefly go back to an issue we discussed just prior to the break. You testified that a commander should take care about the tasks he assigns to undisciplined units, and you have acknowledged that the 4th and 7th Guards Brigades demonstrated undisciplined behaviour in Grahovo. Now, what's your explanation, then, for why General Gotovina was justified to use these two units in taking Knin, which was, as you testified yesterday, the key effort of -- of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my opinion, and obviously I can't speak for General Gotovina, but my opinion, these were the best forces he had in -- in spite of the incidents that he had -- that had been reported to him that had taken place in the ranks. And he needed them, he had trained them, he had infused what junior leadership that he had that had been trained in these two units, and he felt that they could execute the mission. Replacing them on the front line at the time was probably too high risk to achieve his mission and his focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We have to make an occasional break between --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- us because we speak the same language. Are you saying that the Guards Brigades were the -- these two ones I named were the only units capable of taking Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying at the time to continue the operation and the focus of his mission, they were -- I don't say they were the only two that could execute the mission, but there are certainly ones which he knew because he had witnessed their performance, irregardless of the isolated incidents there in Grahovo and other places of some of the soldiers, but he knew the leadership could execute what he intended to do in the next phase of the operation, where, of course, he was focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you call these isolate the incidents when the deputy commander, Ademi, says that, you know, all units participated in these acts except for just two?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the scope of the incidents and the magnitude of them. I know they happened, obviously they were reported. Taking those into the context of 15, 18 months of operation, I think -- I don't have the answer to the question to you [sic] whether those were isolated or whether they were routine. It appeared to be when they were reported, they did happen and now his next mission afoot was taking Knin and continue the offence and that had to be his focus, replacing the units on line at the time probably would have resulted in either delay of the operation or possibly even putting his -- the rest of his forces at risk, as he replaced them in line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's an option a commander could have taken to ask that the operation be postponed, from his perspective?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have, yes. Probably unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Unlikely that his superior, including Tudjman, President Tudjman, would have accepted his proposition.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you got to understand, that even in Operation Storm, he was given four days to complete the operation. That obviously said that time was of essence, and to move forward, the operation was -- was the intent of President Tudjman, the Main Staff, and the minister of defence. By the way, Your Honour, if I may, I could not find the official title, Mr. Cermak in these documents, so if somebody could assist me that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it's important to the case or not, I could not find it in the excerpts I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
