utterances.text: The Chamber has some information about his official title and since, apparently, have you no knowledge of it, we'll not -- at least the Chamber will not pursue the matter at this moment any further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And back to these incidents in Grahovo, you were aware that there were units that were present but did not participate in those activities, undisciplined behaviour. You were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean over units in Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And they could have been used for the main effort to go to Knin.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure you had another regiment. You had two regiments in the sector, the 4th, and 7th. Were you able to mobilise of create another regiment of that size to do that operation, I'd have to look at the composition of units to do determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what other units were there, except for the 4th and the 7th Guards Brigade? And I'm talking about the operation around Grahovo and Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know had you a battalion there which was along those lines, and further to the east you had HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the relationship with General Gotovina and their leadership was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But they could have been used for the attack on Knin, if they were under the command of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have been used if he thought they could have executed the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's go to a couple of other topics. Paragraph 46 in your report talks about the leadership-- General Gotovina that it was present at the decisive points of the operation, providing inspiration and support to the units and soldiers. That's the second -- the third sentence in paragraph 46.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what kind of presence are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, first of all, I cited several things. First of all, earlier on, when he was witnessing the training of his units, he was present to the witnessed that training, look at the curriculum and see how they were trained. As he went through the operation, various instances of him engaging with the commanders. The video was obviously a good reference where, not only was he talking to his commanders in the way at the time at that point to show his displeasure with the success of what he told them and the execution of his intents, but then carried on with them and talked to them about the next mission and how he envision they do that. His flying back to those other units and talking to the commanders is important. I think his -- his basic operation from a forward command post showed that he positioned himself so he could see the battlefield, communicate with commanders, and prepare them for any further change to the mission or change to the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move to paragraph 48, which touches on a related, connected topic. And you -- you say that General Gotovina's role has to be looked at in a wider context. And you mentioned that approximately 30 days after the conclusion of Operation Storm, General Gotovina had to lead another major operation in Bosnia. And then I quote: "The time between Storm and Maestral was short, and General Gotovina's time and efforts would have been dominated by preparations for this next offensive." Now, I think earlier this morning you said you didn't really know in any detail where Gotovina was, you know, during the period, except for a couple of appearances like the video on the 6th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I knew that he was in his forward command post, and I knew that he also flew back to -- to influence the units on the south-western flank to get them moving. I would have -- my assumption, as I said, this -- was General Gotovina, as he was given the next mission, his sector, his line he was responsible for, condensed from about 250 kilometres to 100 kilometres, but added in this next mission was the -- the poor -- the more complex issue now working with another army, the 5th Bosnian Corps, and then continued HVO forces on his right flank and/or Bosnian forces on the other side of them. He now has had added responsibility to coordinate his flanks, coordinate the movement with another army in other sector. So the complexity of the operation where he was fighting for his homeland with people that probably knew very accurately the terrain he is now moving in a 100-kilometre wide sector towards Banja Luka and/or objectives. So the complexity of the strategic and/or operational environment has changed. What I'm referring to here, that period would have focussed him totally to do that coordination, to go talk with the commander of the 5th Corps, the adjacent units to make sure, you know, each -- each unit and their rate of advance and ensure their communication with adjacent units with their fires, with the use of air power so they don't have any fratricide. All those things now have to be considered when you start moving into another phase of your offensive campaign. And still, what I envision is very well time but that momentum they had already achieved had to be sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you were aware that during this period of time between Operation Storm and Maestral, he was often in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware the days or how much time he spent in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps you're aware or made aware that one of the members of his staff testify that he was actually on honeymoon following Operation Storm, in August, were you aware after that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Pretty relaxed commander under these circumstances; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak for him why he did that, why he chose that time. I would expect after fighting for 15 months or so he -- a couple of day he probably was wanted, whether that as a honeymoon or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me continue in paragraph 48. You say: "A noted above, the Croatian military leadership accomplished their mission by providing inspiration and support to their units ..." Now, what do you know about the support of the Croatian leadership? What are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about all the way from the main support staff down. You know, they were obviously involved. They had the resource to support the subordinate commanders. They had to take into account the sectors they were given and who had responsibility and then resource those accordingly. It appeared to me that this was a total focus of the country of Croatia to executed this mission. Obviously the task that they had chosen to do and their vision of the strategic impact of not being successful in these fights, everybody knew that. I think they took a significant risk because of the status and readiness of their young army, and they had to support that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you talk about Croatian military leadership, would you include the Commander-in-Chief of the Croatian Army, President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would -- I would say he is the Commander-in-Chief, yes, in title. He was more of a civil leadership, but I would also include the minister of defence and the other ministers as part of the leadership of the country. Specifically military leadership obviously has to do with each sector, so the Croatian Army -- and how they orchestrated all the way from the -- from the east all the way down to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me tell you what kind of inspiration came down from President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Objection to form, Mr. President. It's not a question. It's a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is still to come, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can rephrase, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you aware that there is evidence in this case that members of the Croatian leadership, expressis verbis, some publicly considered the Serbs a cancer in Croatia. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would there be the kind of support --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considered the Serbs in Croatia a cancer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: A cancer in the body of Croatia. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of inspiration would that be for the troops fighting, according to these support and guidelines in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- this is an argumentative question concerning these issues, I mean, if we want to put the full context of all these comments, and I think if the Chamber has seen quite a bit of the contextualisation of this and it's certainly not the context being put forth by the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not know, Mr. Waespi, whether this expert is better placed to tell us how inspiring certain comments are for troops. Perhaps we would need a psychologist or a sociologist for that. Apart from some common sense, perhaps, might assist in what; but, of course, to give one quote. At the same time, there's nothing wrong with asking what this expert knew at the time he formed his opinions, because this will give an opportunity for the Chamber and for the parties to assess what he has taken into account, what he has considered, when he drew his conclusions. So, therefore, there is nothing wrong with asking whether the witness knew this or knew that. But to ask for the obvious, I must say, a matter which was not uncommon in the whole of the testimony of this witness might not be something to encourage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The reason I was asking is because the witness in his report really ventures out and talks about inspiration and support by the highest leadership, and I wanted to ask him whether he was aware of other comments. That's the reason. And Mr. Kehoe can, in re-examination, put that into a wider context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if in fact we're going contextualise the comments by counsel, then read the question and answer of Ambassador Zuzul that the Prosecution asked. They asked that question and Ambassador Zuzul answered that question, and if that's what we're going to talk about concerning that evidence, let's give the full context of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, as a matter of fact, that would take us another three weeks from now to give the full context and just as the Defence -- if not, perhaps, in every respect give the full context to this witness, whereas the expert had limited material available to form his opinions on. Mr. Waespi, Chamber will consider those matters, and most important is not the view of this witness on whether a certain public speech would be inspiring and what direction, but, rather, whether he knew that this speech was held. And that is a matter which you can certainly explore. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to the last topic, and this is paragraph 43. In paragraph 43, the beginning, you start by saying that: "I cannot refute the fact that undisciplined behaviour occurred in the area of operations," which is a fairly defensive way to put it. You certainly accept that the HV members committed crimes in that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I object to the form. I let it go till he fished, "which is a fairly defensive way to put it," is the Prosecution's characterisation, and I move to strike. If there's a question, that's fine. I object to the speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether -- Mr. Waespi, whether matters are put in a defensive way or not, is -- it's the way in which you use language. Sometimes I say I cannot ignore, but I want to say I know fairly well. That's a way of using language and let's not focus too much on the language and let's focus rather on the substance of what is behind this language.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You accept that the HV committed crimes during the relevant period and the Krajina in 1995. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept the fact that there were crimes committed. Some of them attributed to the HV, the others could have been attributed to either non-combatants, illegal crime, or displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's look at an exhibit. This is P918. It comes out of the command staff of General Gotovina, Split Military District. I want to ask you first whether have you seen this document before. It's dated 12th of August, 1995. And it's written by the assistant commander for political affairs, Captain Mario Tomasovic. And I quote from the middle of the first paragraph: "However, because of the irresponsibility of individual soldiers, non-commissioned officers and officers who comprise the Croatian Army and State through their inappropriate conduct and acts, this success has been partly brought into question." And then it goes on to say: "It is necessary to immediately prevent the following. The continued torching and destruction of facilities and property throughout the entire liberated territory. The killing of live stock; the confiscation of property; inappropriate conduct toward remaining civilians and prisoners of war, and especially towards members and soldiers of the Peace Forces." Now, in your assessment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, I hate to bring up the contextualisation of something, but if we could read the full paragraph, I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, any problem in reading the whole of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not at all. Perhaps the witness is also comfortable to read the document himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Seing as we have it on the record at this point, if counsel can read the full paragraph so he can give that full paragraph, so if anybody is looking at this record down the line, they will see everything, as opposed to the excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I take it it's the second full paragraph starting from, "for this reasons."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "For this reason and following the policy of the Supreme Command commander, Dr. Franjo Tudjman."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "... as well as the instructions by the defence minister and the political administration of the defence ministry of the Republic of Croatia, it is necessary to immediately prevent the following ..." And then we have the four orders. Continues: "In order to implement the above political workers bear special responsibility and are required to inform the unit commanders of the above and take measures to prevent crimes. "In cooperation with the information and security service and the military police, take repressive measures and launch disciplinary procedures against those who do not abide by the instructions. "In conformity with the situation on the ground in your area of responsibility, you are required to follow the guidelines of this warning and, in the realm of political activity, to acquaint all unit members with it. "You're required to submit a report on what has been accomplished by 18 August 1995." And you see to whom all these -- to whom the order or the warning has been addressed. Now, if you were a commander of one of these subordinate units, would you be concerned if you received such a warning?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't think this was a surprise to them. I mean, obviously if you would -- this is coming from the commander of political affairs trying to paint the political picture, strategic picture, I would think these commanders would be also concerned about the same thing. If, in fact, that they thought this was a issue in their area, basically the political advisor to the government is saying, Don't let indisciplined actions overcome the -- you know, the achievements of your units and the reputation which may follow because of indisciplined action. I think that's a good heads up. It is not unlike what the orders had been camming [sic] out by General Gotovina, and, in fact, it re-enforces that. As you see, it is sent directly to the three OPs groups and information sent to him. So I think it is a reiteration of the fact that, Hey, guys, pay attention, and this could have a long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, let me stop you here. Why not answer the question? I mean, you're telling us whether it came as a surprise; you're telling us about what you would do. The question simply was: If you were a commander of one of these subordinate units, would you be concerned if you received such a warning? Mr. Waespi clearly wants to know whether this is a worrying message [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't do -- consider this a warning. I consider this a -- you know, a heads up that say, you know, pay attention. This is -- we're not -- it's not something as a surprise to these commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's called a warning. So you would say you interpret this as an encouraging measure rather than an alarm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. It is reinforcing the fact of the importance of continuing to -- to -- to execute and not allow indisciplined behaviour within your ranks caused outside international perspective of the value of Croatian military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Mr. Waespi apparently wants to know is whether the situation, which, apparently, called for such a reinforcements, whether that was a worrying situation, yes or no. That's, I think, the core of his question. Mr. Waespi, please correct me when I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And I believe on line 18, you did say, "I do not consider this a warning." Is that what you said? Because you were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it may be semantics. I don't think it's a warning from to the commanders. This is coming from a political advisor. You know, he has -- is simply stating a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think you testified yesterday that you were commanding units up to the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I commanded that and I also commanded the Aviation Warfighting Center at Fort Rucker, two-star level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many warnings like that you have received as a commander in your command functions?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we don't have a political advisor, political affairs. A message would have come down through command channels reinforcing the fact about the incidents we were talking about. It would not have come from a political advisor in the US Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you have never received a warning or encouragement like that addressing these topics here, that actions of your unit compromise the -- your army and your state through inappropriate conduct on acts. Have you received a warning like that in your career?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: By the way, is it the first time you see this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I have not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move to a second example, and I think you have seen this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is P1140.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: A document dated 19th August. Let me quote it as full as I can. It's authored by Colonel Mladen Fuzul.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Counsel, if I can be of assistance, it is in tab 17 of the General's binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's a very short document.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel Fuzul writes, and he is an OG commander: "Due to the observed breakdown of order and discipline and for the international reputation of the Republic of Croatia, I hereby order: 1, establish supervision in all units and immediately take measures against the torching of buildings and the killing of animals. 2, take disciplinary and criminal measures against irresponsible individuals. 3, the commanders of OG West units are responsible to me for the implementation of this order." Now, how alarming for you as a commander is it to receive information about a breakdown of order and discipline. Do you see that again as an encouragement?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think this is what you see is a chain of events and this is in Colonel Fuzul reinforcing some of the things you just showed and emphasising as we come into a -- a -- a point in this operation that this will not be tolerated. I think this -- and he specifically as a commander is giving this to his specific elements to make sure that they understand that, so this is passing that information further down in a subsequent order to make sure they understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this order comes a week, seven days, after the warning from Colonel Tomasovic. And it almost repeats the language of what happened, you know, the killing of animals, the torching of buildings. Would you consider that the first order, or the first warning, 12th August, was ineffective, if a week later, just another order has to be issued? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see this as a separate order. I see it -- a reinforcements in the orders in the chain. If you also go back to the 10th of August, General Gotovina also issued a similar order to his subordinate units to stop indisciplined behaviour. Then you had from the political staff the issue of talking about the potential reputation of the Croatian Army and that, and now you see at the brigade level this commander coming out, albeit, I think, several days later, reiterating the fact that it could be reputation but even more important take disciplinary measures against -- I know what a criminal measure may be, but take disciplinary measures about indiscipline and actions and events. I think that is necessary to reinforce the chain of orders here to get focus by these troops all the way down. If you look at it in the big picture at this time what is happening after Storm and you have had a lot of troop movements and now you've got a lot of people moving on battlefield and probably the risk of anything indisciplined happen was you -- these soldiers envisioned freedom of movement is probably peaking at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Look what we have. We have the video --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- of the 6th of August, of the commander turning to his subordinate commanders. We have a couple of written orders. We have a warning of a political person, who is also concerned about the reputation to the state, addresses the shortcomings.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we may have an order of the 10th of August. And then on 19th of August, another order. Apparently nothing happens. The commanders don't discipline soldiers, activity continues. Isn't that what we have to read from the sequence of these orders and, indeed, this last document, P1140?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you could interpret it that way, but I do not interpret it that way. I see a sequence of orders, and I think following this particular date, you'll see an increase in the number of -- of -- of arrests, investigations, and finding people culpable for all offences. So I think this series, from approximately the 4th of August on, or, actually, the 30th July on to this period, now is really getting the commanders at all levels to focus and people in -- not only in the forward forces but also in the rear areas, focussed on getting control of indisciplined conduct. Now, I can't tell you what the scope of all that is by reading the documents here, but certainly there is things that -- happening that need to re-establish law and order in the rear and re-establish the country as was once known under the constitutional authority. At the same time this was happening, obviously General Gotovina and some of his forces were also continuing the fight. So this is a -- a -- a point of emphasis to get control of indisciplined measures that simultaneously what was happening, his focus on the fight forward, and that agreement with Bosnia and so forth. So you got dual focuses here. Here to get this under control but continue the fight. And you see General Gotovina and his staff also kind of caught in the middle of this and his commanders. So somebody has got to pick up and pay attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could I seek one further specification. You said -- you'll see an increase in the number of addresses, investigations, and finding people culpable and you said following this particular date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Following this period of enforcing the need to take disciplinary action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what's the source exactly of this observation about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a report from military police commander backed up, I believe, Mr. Lausic, stating the number of arrests, the number of conviction, and what they have been able to accomplish based on all the things that happened here to show control of the area and reinforcement of the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other sources or just this one, then we can check it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the one I read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one you read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my question and obviously as how I saw that: How come the field commanders didn't see that same report because it went up through Mr. Lausic and minister of the interior's channels not through the commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As an officer of the court, Judge, I also have to tell you that we provided the General in our discussions with the substance of Mr. Theunens' testimony, and without reading that testimony I'll just give the reference points. It's mainly on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but did you give the report to the witness or did you -- you just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... read the -- what you consider to be the relevant portions [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Read these portions of the testimony, which I'll tell Your Honour what the reading of it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact -- I think that it has been expressed several times that transparency in sources and facts assumed was of vital importance comes as a bit of a surprise that it's nowhere said, I think here, that selection of -- selection made by counsel was read to me and that -- but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Judge, this is cross-examination, of course, I didn't bring out this number during the course of my direct examination concerning what Mr. Theunens said concerning the increase in discipline. And I believe he says the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we don't have to repeat it. I asked the witness what his source was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'm just trying to be as transparent as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to more or less [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I read by giving you the page without reading the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So say the answer of the witness is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying it's incorrect at all. I'm not saying that it is incorrect at all. All I'm saying in the spirit of candor with the Chamber, the issue of the number of disciplinary proceedings came up in the source of our discussion, and I will tell you as an officer of the court I relayed to the witness during our discussions what Mr. Theunens said about that increase, which is in the transcript, which I will provide, Your Honour, without going into the particular number. Now, I did not elicit that during the course of my direct examination. But I will -- I will say over the course of the several days that we were talking prior to Monday that subject did, in fact, come up and he mentions that number on page 12576.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I -- Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So we have seen this document on the 19th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Apparently, you know, the same situation after seven days, despite whatever efforts other people might have done on the ground, whether you were correctly informed or not. Let's go to another document, which is D654?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would object to that comment going from "apparently" or to "you were correctly informed" or not as, again, a speech and not a question and move to strike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If could I say something -- one thing, Mr. Counsel, this one order you are referring to only goes to a select number of units not -- it's not an OG. It's just a brigade and elements. So to me that's why I saw it was reinforcing the importance of the string of orders from the highest level now down to the brigade level. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But it's -- I'm not sure I understand you. But this is the OG commander issuing an order to all -- appears to me of his subordinate units, which includes the 112th Brigade, 113th Brigade, the 7th Home Guard Regiment and a couple of other units.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Coming down now you see the OG is another subordinate of the other elements. I know that the -- the political advisor had advised him, but also going back, he had also been told several times. And so now he is reiterating the fact in writing. It doesn't say he had not already verbally told them to do this days earlier so now in the follow-up written order obviously you have a documented case where he has told his subordinates in writing to -- to correct the indisciplined behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But why would he issue a written order on the 19th of August, 1995, which is a serious one, if the situation, you know, doesn't warrant it anymore, because it's okay on the ground or because he has told his commanders already orally? Why would he sit down and draft an order like that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't know what he was doing between the 12th and the 10th and the 19th. Or even if he was not even present and had them to approve this, so I don't know what led up or why the lateness in now publishing a written order on the 19th. So I'm not sure I could understand that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But the obvious reading of this document is there is a serious issue happening which needs to be corrected on the 19th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could interpret it that way. You could also interpret that the orders previously on 10th and 12th also stated the same thing and he is just now following under his command getting the written directive out. So whatever delay that was, you know, you could interpret it whether you see there is still a problem, but I see it in a course -- it's a delay in him publishing an order to his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Frankly that is an interesting interpretation. Why do you choose that over my interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I don't know. I wasn't there. I don't know what delayed him, you know -- I have seen orders come out by subordinates a week later or so because they weren't there to approve the order. His staff may have written the order, and it didn't get published by the 19th. He may have verbally stated the order earlier but just now on the 19th it gets published. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, may I just try to understand your testimony. Mr. Waespi puts to you that the order had to be repeated because it was ineffective; that's apparently his position. You say, No, I interpret it as being a delay in writing down the order and further sending into the chain of command. That's -- if I well understood your different interpretations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot solely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now Mr. Waespi asks you, Why is your interpretation better than mine? And then you answer that question that you do not know because you do not know what caused the delay. Now what you say is, The reason why mine is better is because it's mine. Because if you say, I do not know what caused the delay, that suggests, clearly, that it was a delayed putting on paper of the order that it was not, as Mr. Waespi's position is, it wasn't a repeated order because the earlier one to be ineffective. So by invoking, not knowing the reasons for the delay, you exclude for the possibility that it was anything else than a delay. Therefore, when you are explaining why your interpretation is better than Mr. Waespi's, you're invoking that your interpretation is the right one; it was a delay. I'm putting this to you because I want to find out exactly the methods, methodology of interpretation of these kind of things, and, therefore, I think it's fair that I put this to you so that can you respond and tell me why this is not, as I suggested to you, a logical flaw in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me give you this analogy. If I'm one your subordinate commanders and I published an order on the 10th of August telling that you indisciplined behaviour must stop, on the 12th and I have that in writing. On 12th of August, I get the note from the general council talking about reputational impact of indisciplined behaviour, which reinforces the order I just got from my boss saying to stop this. For me to wait a week to take action by publishing a subsequent order after you just told me that in writing or even not only a week, nine days, would be irresponsible behaviour on my part. That's why I -- I can't fathom why a person would wait to the 19th to publish an order nor can I conclude that the -- that the indisciplined behaviour got worse and that as the counsel had said that this says that the -- a conclusive piece of evidence that we still had to do something else. You've already told me it's bad and fix it on 10th of August. Now whatever I've done between that date and publish an order to document I did something, I don't know what that time, you know, because I wasn't there. That was my logic but you, as my boss, I would have done something very quickly if you gave me a written order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, carefully listening to your answer, your actual answer to Mr. Waespi's question was, therefore, I don't know why my interpretation is any better than yours. However, your answer was explaining why your interpretation was better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to analyse carefully the way of thinking and the logic involved in the conclusions you draw. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to another order issue by, I believe, the same commander. This is D654. And it dates the 31st of August, 1995. And as you -- yes, we see on the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can go to the English on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You will see that somebody signs for the OG West commander, Colonel Fuzul. But let's go to the contents again on page 1. So here, on the 31st of August, we have the OG West commander, again, issuing an order, and I quote: "1, commanders of Split Military District units in their zones of responsibility in newly liberated territory of the RH shall take all necessary measures to ensure that all military infrastructure facilities are placed under full supervision and protection. "Stop all devastation, regardless of what the facility's purpose is (barracks, depot, training ground, residential building, and so forth)." Second paragraph: "Before putting into operation the new facilities in the newly liberated territory, conduct planned and organised explosives and demolition inspections, and use the skilled and authorised persons to the units [sic] to dispose of explosives." And for the sake of completion, paragraph 3: "The Split Military District Command has initiated a proposal to the HV Main Staff for the handover of certain civilian facilities to the owners for protection and guarding, such as the pontoon bridge, the Obrovac hydroelectric power, the Muskovci water pumping station, and the Promina radio and TV transmitter. "The HV will continue to guard these facilities until this matter is resolved at the level of the superior commander and with the relevant state bodies." Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel, if I may. Insistent with Mr. Waespi's comment on 123 [sic] in the spirit of completion if we could read the preamble that sets forth the purpose of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the order of the Split Military District commander," classification number, file number, "of 29 August 1995 and for the purposes of protecting military property, I hereby order ..." So now, again, over a week later to the previous document, we have the same person, or somebody signing for him, ordering his subordinate units, Stop all devastation. And it goes on to say that it includes residential buildings. Again, the insubordination or indisciplined behaviour or the crimes or whatever you want to call it continues, despite issuing written orders or whatever actions might have taken place. Do you agree with the interpretation I put to you in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the document once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you spin that up --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You can also have my copy, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My hard copy, I'm happy to provide it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can you put --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you move down, I can't see the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is that you can't look at two pages at the same time. Therefore, you're provided with the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And you asked me for my interpretation of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Whether my interpretation was correct, that all these efforts, mainly the written efforts, as we see from these orders, were ineffective because the indisciplined behaviour goes on, requiring the commander, at the end of August, I believe, to issue a very, very strong order, Stop all devastation. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you only in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I -- can you elaborate?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. No doubt, you know, when we talk about the liberated areas, now we've reached a phase which they must reclaim some of the structure to include military barracks, depots and so forth. My interpretation of this looting and actions such as that continue in all the areas because the military had evacuated these or moved forward. Now they must reclaim those facilities. I -- I come to that conclusion because -- because before putting in new facilities, as stated in paragraph 2, conduct planned and organised explosives and demolition, so they must clear the buildings. At some risk there may have been explosives in those buildings either because of occupancy of someone else before -- you know, before they moved throughout the area or now as they regained those, or somebody else's indiscriminate use of -- so they've got to clear the building and take precautions. So that doesn't necessarily correspond to me that military people are looting or doing those actions. It could be a combination of other people, but it's a matter of reclaiming those and then protecting them so they would have the infrastructure to have a military in the future. So I think it is a pretty good order. I think it's good thing to do and probably comes at the right time. It also says, in the end, some of the facilities must be returned over, such as civilian facilities to the rightful owners. That's my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you would -- or do you agree with me that, until this point at least, devastation goes on?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that there is indiscriminate or indisciplined behaviour, and probably looting continued in the rear areas at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is done by members of the HV?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So why would Colonel Fuzul tell his subordinates to stop all devastation, if it was done by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I mean, I would like to address this outside the presence of the witness, and it might -- my question goes to the good faith basis for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a second. Since everyone speaks English, Mr. Jones, including you, we can't just do with taking off your earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I'm not so sure I speak English. I've been [indiscernible] through counsel a couple of times. Yes, sir, I will be right back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this order, and I was going to get into this as opposed to on redirect examination, but I felt it incumbent to bring this to the Court's attention outside of the presence of the witness when we get into this. This order, as can you see in D964, has a line there that -- excuse me, D654, has a line that goes back to the Split Military District commander order. If the Prosecution checked their own system, the Split Military District order is written in exactly verbatim the same fashion and it comes from an order from the HV Main Staff which is exactly the same as set forth in Colonel Fuzul's order. So comes from Cervenko, verbatim it's given back out by Gotovina, and verbatim it's given back out by Fuzul. That is what the chain of command is here. As opposed to this line coming from a question, So why would Colonel Fuzul tell his subordinates to stop all the devastation? Colonel Fuzul is following orders coming down the chain of command and I submit to Your Honour that this -- this information is in the possession of the Prosecutor. Ergo, the -- I challenge the good faith basis for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to me there are several possible explanations of how this happened, and, therefore, the Prosecution may ask the witness why this was done this way. I mean, if, over a certain period of time the devastation would have stopped immediately, you would have expected some other action rather than sipping through -- but let's not -- let's not at this moment discuss the -- how we would evaluate and interpret this evidence. Let's focus exclusively on what is admissible to ask to the witness and the question, as such, which -- and that may be clear, Mr. Waespi, seems not to pay a lot of attention to the verbatim repetition of words. In whatever way we would have to interpret that, there are many ways of interpreting that, is admissible, but I take it that you're aware that if you ignore that element that it might come back as a boomerang at a later stage. There is no -- no reason at this moment to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just want to advise in the true spirit this order that comes from General Cervenko goes to the Military Districts in Zagreb, Karlovac, Bjelovar, Gospic, Split, the navy, the air force, and the air defence system, plus the archive. It goes to everybody that is in the military system and filtered down, and the only thing that General Gotovina, I submit to Your Honour, is doing is ordering, giving an order out that Cervenko, General Cervenko, has given to everybody. Now, the question that I can object that I can object to this was the contextualisation of that, as if this is an isolated the incident that Colonel Fuzul is doing by himself, without providing the context to the witness. Now I know that you can't provide the context to everything, Judge, or we would be here for a month. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, make it three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the intervention by Mr. Kehoe at least puts you on notice and does not -- let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can ask him a couple of questions actually along the lines of what is suggested by Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I consulted with my colleagues, Mr. Waespi. We'd like to hear from you, if I use my own words, which -- why you risk the boomerang. What's your response to what Mr. Kehoe tells us?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe that the issue is whether a commander would issue an order if he knew that in his area of responsibility there was no issue about devastation, there was absolutely no issue. Why would in order -- issue such a serious thing if he knows, you know, his area, his command is free from that. So he is certainly not -- not a puppet, not a machine. Mr. Fuzul would certainly check first with his subordinate people. He knows what is happening in his area, and if there is no issue in relation it that, I'm sure he would resist from issuing this order. So it's just repeating what is coming down to the bottom of the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say, verbatim or not, to further put an order down the hierarchical lines if the situation on the ground would not justify such an order to be further sent down the chain of command, that you would expect a strong protest against an order to issue a totally unjustified order for your area of responsibility. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Of course, he has to be sure that there was no devastation in his area. Otherwise he has a problem. Because then he doesn't follow directions from his superior people. But if he knows, There is no devastation in my area, I'm sure a responsible commander wouldn't issue an order like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the objection. Mr. Waespi is allowed to proceed as he did. At the same time, Mr. Waespi, it -- you're now put on notice of what the concerns of Mr. Kehoe are. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: General, to provide you with a larger background or context to this document which I had to take back, unfortunately -- actually, I can give it to you again. Apparently the reference to the order of the Split Military District, above the word "order," it says "pursuant to order," this relates to an -- apparently an identical order which, in fact, was issued a level above the Military District by the main commander, Commander-in-Chief, General Cervenko, addressing, issuing this order to all Military Districts who, in turn, then, you know, order their subordinate units. So take it in the context of this is a verbatim order from higher commanders. Now, under what circumstances would you issue this order to your subordinate units, tell them to stop devastation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, that -- I would do this to -- to ensure that whatever state at the time our facility are that we stop any further degradation of those facilities by whatever is happening. If in fact barracks, depots, training areas and so forth had suffered some or continued to suffer some deterioration, I'd like that stopped immediately, to offset the cost of re-establishing those in the future. So the point here being, stop all devastation. Now you're asking your military units to stop that, not particularly to me implying that they are the ones doing it, but whoever is doing it to protect those facilities so that we can re-establish them in the future. But as you take on and look at those facilities, make sure clear them of any ordnance that may be in there. So, you know, obviously throughout the country at this time there is a concern of any continued deterioration of government facilities. That's the way I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now when you say that the point here is to stop all devastation, do you have any information that the military was authorised to intervene, you know, if other people would -- would devastate these buildings?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously they have by the virtue of this order, you know, this is on government -- if they're talking about barracks, if they're talking about training facilities, residential buildings that belong to the military, they have the authority - that's federal property - to intervene to protect those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It -- actually doesn't say for military purposes here, at least not in -- in that sentence we look at; stop all devastation. It just talks about regardless of what the facility's purpose is, barracks, depot, training ground, residential buildings, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The context might be wider and can be explored in re-examination, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I object to the -- I object to the premise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I try not to speak at the same time. If others would do that as well. Then at least the transcript could be complete. Mr. Kehoe, it was clear to you from my eye contact that once Mr. Waespi would have finished his question I would have allowed you to make an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President, and to the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You, Mr. Waespi, you already ruled on an objection you expected before even the Chamber could hear it. Well, a lot was said today about undisciplinary behaviour. It was suggested that undisciplinary behaviour raises some concerns. It does. Would you please finish your question. Then Mr. Kehoe will have an opportunity to object to it. And then the proper authority to rule on it will do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My question to you, General, was that in that sentence I want you to focus on, but you could look at it in a context, it only talks about stopping all devastation, regardless of what the facility's purpose is, barracks, depot, training ground, residential building, and so forth. So when you interject that residential buildings are buildings used or owned by the military, that's your interpretation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- contextualisation again is it goes back to the preamble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I don't even -- Mr. Waespi, paragraph 1 of this order refers to all military infrastructure facilities are placed under supervision and protection. Second paragraph orders to stop all devastation, regardless of what the facility's purpose is. Now, please tell me what the reference to facility in paragraph 2 could be, other than a reference to the facilities mentioned in the order under number 1? If you want to spend a lot of time on it, we'll have to ask Mr. Jones to leave the courtroom. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I accept your point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have one last issue, and this is the Ademi appointment on the 3rd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It will take about ten minutes, Mr. President. I don't know whether we want to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I would like to discuss scheduling before we have the break, in view of the wish expressed by Mr. Cayley to examine the witness also for 30 minutes. If you can guarantee with the assistance of Mr. Kehoe that you will need not more than ten minutes, we'll now finish your cross-examination and then have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Even with the assistance and perhaps because of the assistance of Mr. Kehoe, I cannot guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, can you finish your -- in ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll try to do it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to call D793, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, would you like this back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you General. Now, this is the -- now I think almost famous order of the 3rd of August which plays, apparently, a central role in your argument that General Gotovina acted properly and reasonably. And you remember, it's the removal of Colonel Slaven Zdilar. You certainly remember the document from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's have a look at this document again. Now, first of all, it's -- the first time you have seen this document was on -- on Sunday, because I understand it's not quoted or cited by you in your report. Is that correct? Footnote 47 is the key footnote where this document that suggests you should have been quoted.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: 47 in my report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you it's not quoted there.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me, and you have given your explanation yesterday and I think today as well, that in this order replacing the commander of OG North there is no indication that it was done in response to undisciplined behaviour in -- in end of July. There's no reference here to that effect. I know you interpret the purpose of having a uniform command and control of the units in a certain way but there is no reference to -- to, you know, some indisciplined units. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree on the base document. And could I expand on that, if you like, why I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not at this moment. Now, were you shown by the Defence, Mr. Kehoe and his colleagues, any information why, more specific information than what is contained in the document, of why Colonel Zdilar had to be removed?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the standpoint of my examination of the document in discussing with them the series of events of which units underneath OG North had -- had demonstrated indisciplined behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you have no information that any disciplinary or other proceedings were initiated against Colonel Zdilar for not having control of his units?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time. At this time, on the eve of the Operation Storm he was removed, and that in itself is a form of disciplinary action from my perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But he's, at the same time, appointed to a fairly senior staff position as chief of infantry. You accept that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yeah, and that to me, from a military perspective, is moved to the rear and into a support or an institutional job not an operational job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So are you saying General Gotovina doesn't trust this commander anymore?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation of this is he doesn't have the confidence that he can command and control his units or his subordinate units which put the operation at risk and the fact that there was probably a series of events leading up to this which caused him to take that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 7389, an order by General Gotovina dated 22nd September 1995. And you see here that it's General Gotovina reappointing Colonel Zdilar as an OG commander. If you go down in the English to the bottom, you see the OG West command is formed in the following structure, OG West commander Slaven Zdilar, brigadier. Number 1, General Gotovina reappoints a person he allegedly had to remove because he couldn't control his units. This person is even promoted as a higher rank than before. And, as you can see from (b), just above the appointment, he now controls one OG which is a combination of OG South and West, so clearly an important position. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I object to the last characterization of important position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can take that back. No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, a position. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, General, from the perspective of your report's key topics, command climate and condoning undisciplined behaviour of subordinates, what message would that send to his subordinates if, first, General Gotovina removes the commander because of disciplinary shortcomings, and then the next month he reappoints this commander, even in a promoted fashion, and installs him basically into the same function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to the -- I don't know if there's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's -- yes, briefly say what your objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if -- if counsel is aware of what happened in between or he's just left that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can explore that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can that at a later stage, if you think that the matter is -- but, again, from my next question to the witness it may appear that the reasons to explore that might be not that big. First of all, Mr. Jones, from you aware of this appointment in September of Mr. Zdilar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was not. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you answer my question? What message does that send to -- to his subordinate troops, to remove somebody first, accepting your explanation that it was done because he wasn't trusted anymore, couldn't do his job, and then to reappoint him, even in a promoted fashion?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd -- obviously when he's cited for the unity of command and control, as the case may be at that time, my -- my interpretation of that was -- was that he had -- he did not see the -- the sequence of his orders and his intent being carried out in his subordinate commanders and he replaced him. Now for whatever reason he elected to give him another opportunity is stated here later on. I would have to have the background. I do not know. I'm not sure it's a promotion. I would have to look back and see if he's at the same grade, but, however, this looks like a reorganising, restructuring of the forces and giving him OG West command once again, with a supporting structure of someone who has also been an OG commander in Fuzul, it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I suggest to that you there are two options here. Either the first removal on the 3rd of August --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- had nothing to do with disciplinary issues. And then your central document, which is this D793, does not support your theory that these disciplinary issues were correctly assessed by General Gotovina. Or we have here General Gotovina rewarding undisciplined behaviour. Do you agree that these are the two options we have?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- the latter part about rewarding undisciplined behaviour, I don't think is why he relieved him. The undisciplined behaviour was the insubordinate units, but the ability for him to carry out his orders and his intent would be more in line why he would have been relieved. Now, the incidents of indisciplined behaviour in his unit were indicative of him being able to command and control his units. Now -- so I don't know if I can correlate to rewarding undisciplined behaviour by doing this. However, it's not uncommon, from my perspective, sometimes to see if someone did have a leadership flaw and you didn't have a lot of resources to draw from in the past, and you had to form another command to potentially giving that person another chance because he just, at the point in time, may have been mentally fatigued; and so you try to re-energise him, give him some supporting cast to make him successful. We don't want to tear a leadership down forever, but if he warrants another opportunity, maybe that's what happened. I don't know. I don't know the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You don't know the circumstances so you actually don't know what the reasons were for relieving Colonel Zdilar in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was referring -- I don't why he gave him another command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But you also don't know why he was relieved in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than what he stated of an effective unity of command which implies his ability to carry out his orders as either written or his intent the commander had given him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. We will have a break but we will already invite to you be escorted out the courtroom, Mr. Jones. I do understand that you have plans to travel tomorrow morning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- we'll try to see whether matters can be scheduled in such a way that it would not prevent you from travelling tomorrow. How disastrous would it be if we would not be able to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To depart tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously I'm at your, you know, disposal. I would have to change some things back in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's not -- you're missing the marriage of your daughter or a reception by the president of the United States.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I omitted to tender 65 ter 7389. That's the last document I have shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reappointment document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2618.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I'm looking at Mr. Cayley. You said you would need 30 minutes. Would that be the best, Mr. Kehoe, that Mr. Cayley would go first in this respect as a kind of a delayed cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We've actually agreed, Mr. President, that Mr. Kehoe is going to go first, because it may actually abbreviate what I have to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's good to hear that you have considered the practical consequences of the order in which you examine the witness. Mr. Kehoe, could you give us an indication as to how much time would you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would say, Mr. President, about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour. Mr. Cayley, would it still be half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can we see what Mr. Kehoe does and then I can certainly let you know. I'll do my best. I understand the point you're making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Chamber may have questions as well. I'm just considering at this moment what possibilities there are to have an extended session and to continue this afternoon. Now, half an hour plus half an hour would bring us beyond a quarter to 2.00. That's clear. Let me ask the Registrar about the results of his inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are, as always, invited to be as efficient as possible in the use of their time. We'll resume at ten minutes past 1.00. Then we would have left 35 minutes, which would not cover the time requested. There is not yet a definitive green light for a session this afternoon, a session which, I suggest, would start ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now have green light for one session this afternoon, which means that after the break we'll see how far we come. We'll stop at a quarter to 2.00, have a one-hour lunch break and have one session on from a quarter to 3.00 onwards. The danger of having time available is that it will be used. We ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, you will now be re-examined by Mr. Kehoe. You may proceed Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, good afternoon. I would like to -- I would like to go through a series of topics, not everything that was covered on cross, but I'd like to cross-examination -- I would like to discuss the last topic first concerning Colonel Zdilar. And we have on the screen, as can see is P2618, which is putting now Brigadier Zdilar in as the commander in OG West on 22nd September, 1995. Now, you noted two things in your testimony yesterday. Number one, this is on page 20933, line 5 to 6, that General Gotovina didn't have a lot of resources to replace commanders with. And today, on page 85, on line 9 and 10, you said that: "We don't want to tear a leadership down forever and if he warrants another opportunity, maybe that's what happened." Now, General, bringing a person back by General Gotovina would be -- would it be an attempt by a commander to rehabilitate that person?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a couple of documents that pre-date the appointment of Zdilar on 22 of September, and I want to show you two documents that you have not seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And one is 65 ter -- excuse me, 1D2945.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you these two documents, General, before we go into this. General, this is a document that is the 21st of August, 1995, and it comes from General Gotovina. Notes that: "Due to the demonstrated need and for the continuity of command and control of units in the Split Military District ... I hereby ... all appointments to the position of commander of OG West are hereby suspended; and 2, I hereby temporarily appoint the commander of the 113th Infantry Brigade, Colonel Danijel Kotlar as acting commander of OG West." It says the order takes effect the next day. And before we go into the next document, I'd like to offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1636.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can we can put on the screen -- thank you, Mr. President. If we can put on the screen 1D2946.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this is an order three days, again signed by General Gotovina on the 24th of August, 1995. Talking about the temporary command of OG West: "Due to the demonstrated need to acquire insight, regulate the situation, and ensure continuity in commanding OG West, I hereby order, the temporary command of OG West shall be formed with the following composition. Colonel Danijel Kotlar," the individual we looked at in previous exhibit, "representative of the commander of OG West. Brigadier Slaven Zdilar as the Chief of Staff." Now, General, if you were going to bring somebody back in to give them a second chance, would you put them in a primary position or would you put them in a Chief of Staff position to see how that person performs when you do bring them back.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously you have the option to that. You would want to see if he can perform, but you also may be doing this to get his head back into the game of the operation. You wouldn't just want to put him back in cold, so the Chief of Staff position is obviously one which he would be able to -- to regain his knowledge of the operation, probably the quickest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 1D2946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1637.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, the order that we saw previously, the P2618 and that was the 22nd of September, 1995, which puts Brigadier Zdilar in command of OG West command and this is, of course, based on the testimony you talked about previously as prior to Operation Southern Move. As further trying to give this person a chance, sir, would you put that person in a role that was not the most difficult role in the world or would you throw him right in and put him in the most difficult role possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] ... all leading questions. Could be probably asked, What role would you give him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The role -- that question, I believe, is in the disjunctive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. It is to some extent leading, of course, the showing of the documents, of course, assists greatly as well. I have a bigger concern, that is, looking at the document and asking whether you would expect this document to be delivered on a sunny day or on a rainy day, well, of course, you would look at whether the paper is wet and then conclude that it must have been a rainy day. It is the speculative and that's true for the testimony itself, to some extent, to the questions put by Mr. Waespi, and your questions as well, Mr. Kehoe, is the level of -- of coming close to speculation is -- is worrying me a bit. Could you please keep that in mind when you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I'd like to move to the actual order for the operation in Southern Move, and that would be 65 ter 5531. And it has a variety of pieces of information but if we can go to page 9 in the English, and it's 9 in the B/C/S as well, I'm informed. And I realise that you don't have a hard copy of this, General, but if can you take a look at this document -- excuse me, it's page 4 in the English, I'm informed. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you're referring to tasks for units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tasks for individual units. It gives a task for the 7th Guards Brigade on page 9. And if we go to page 10, that continues on, these being combat tasks. I'm not going to read it because obviously you can see there, combat tasks. Page 11, paragraph 5.42, other information given to the 4th Guards Brigade. And then there were a series of units that get combat activities. And if we could turn to page 16 of the English, when we talk about the tasks of Operative Group West over which Brigadier Zdilar is in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that's in 7 in the -- page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
