utterances.text: Now, General, you see the role given to Operative Group West for Operation Southern Move and this is the order signed by General Gotovina. And, actually, signed by General Ademi on behalf of General Gotovina. Would you consider this particular role, based on your knowledge of Operation Southern Move, a minor role for someone who was being brought back into -- to prove himself?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this point in time, if I remember, it was now three operational groups versus four?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right sir.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Operations Group North is leading the main effort; west is obviously on the flank and going into a defensive assignment. Of the three areas where you've got east, which is doing a defence in zone and obviously a passage of lines to introduce forces for the attack. I interpreted this: You've had two OP groups forward and the north will past through east and continue the attack. So obviously the three operational groups west has the lesser complexity of assignments, just my interpretation of what I have seen. So -- I looked at the previous order and also the words in there about correcting the current situation of assignments, to me that must have been something to the effect of re-setting and reorganising the forces and task organisation under the group. That was ongoing when -- the General Zdilar, or Brigadier Zdilar was appointed the Chief of Staff so he could orchestrate that and formulate that plan, then he was appointed as commander. So he had become part of the plan and so forth. Now, his experience previous -- probably earlier on, prior to his relief, showed some -- some probably talent and capability of doing it, and that's probably why he got this command and that responsibility. I don't know why the previous commander of Operation Group West was then delineated as the deputy. That is my interpretation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer 65 ter 5531 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1638.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm going shift topics, and I just want to ask you a few comments about some of your testimony about General Cermak, and you noted on page 46, lines 12 to 21, that you had no knowledge of General Cermak's title. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when we go to D1632, which is the tasking order that it was given -- tasking letter that was given to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could put that up on the screen. And if we can go to the next -- looking that page and the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the tasking letter as well as the appendix with the facts, there was no request of you to analyse the duties and responsibilities of the role of General Cermak, was there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were not provided any orders or other documents signed and drafted by General Cermak, were you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now if we can go to your book and look at the tabs. And we look at tab 3, 4, and 5. And under tabs 3, 4, 5, we have the order by General -- D409, which is 2nd August 1995 order by General Lausic. D269, the 3 August 1995 orders by Lausic, re the cooperation between the minister -- the military police and the Ministry of the Interior. And lastly, D1634, which were the minutes of the closed session of the Croatian government. Would it be fair to say, General, those were the three documents that you relied upon to take the position that you did in your -- in your report where this law enforcement was going to be transited back to the institutional order of the Republic of Croatia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which paragraph are we talking about, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will give you the exact paragraph, Mr. President. It is actually mentioned in several locations. One is paragraph 8. Another is -- excuse me, paragraph 21, where the -- the last sentence, for instance, in paragraph 21 says: "As a result, it was not up to the HV operational commanders to regulate the transition of responsibility for law and order in that area."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it is obvious what the purpose is, but I think it is an important, potentially important area if the witness could be asked, you know, what did you rely upon when you expressed those opinions, rather than pointing him to what, you know, he might have relied upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I think it would be apparently the issue of sources and factual basis is important, so to the extent you could refrain from leading --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer your question counsel, yes, these are three -- but it seems to me there was one other document which specified in the -- in the order from the Main Staff, re-emphasising the minister of the interior and/or the ability to discuss the reestablishment of civilian territories from, and I don't know exactly what, but that's -- this is the genesis of what that also said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And would you be referring to, if we can turn to -- excuse me. That would be tab 5, D1634, which on page 7 is General Jarnjak talking about when the army enters the area, the military police follows, et cetera. Do you recall that? It's about three lines --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It also shows by their -- the numbers of which were available and which he discusses diverting to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, to get a full assessment of General Cermak's duties and responsibilities, would you have to review a series of documents in which he was involved as well as all his orders in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Plus his task organisation, how he planned to execute the responsibilities given to him which I didn't look at in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you did not do any of those items in this case because were not asked to do so?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let me shift topics once again, and if I can go back and just show you D654, which is the Fuzul order concerning the military property dated 31 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you just took the witness to D1634. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 654. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, the previous one I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe that's 16 -- D1634, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what page did you take him to, because it goes over --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I took him to page -- if I may, Mr. President, it's page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 7 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The item that we've referenced is about four lines from the top that begins mid sentence: "But ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I'd just like to address you to this particular document, dated 31 August, by Colonel Fuzul, and refer to the preamble when it notes that: "Pursuant to the order of the Split Military District commander" -- and it gives a number and a file number 1080-01-95-74 of 29 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me. Are you waiting for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translation, sir --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- to try and catch up. I would like to refer you back to that document with the 1080-01-94-174 document, which is 1D2947. [Microphone not activated] This is an order from the 29th of August --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 29th of August. And that document refers to another order from the Chief of Staff. And this is signed by General Gotovina. As we can see, this is a -- taking a look at that it is an exact copy of Colonel Fuzul's order. And then if we could go to the beginning order from the Main Staff from the 25th -- excuse me, the 25th of August, 1995; that would be 1D2948. And note this is a -- the 25th of August, 1995, signed by General Cervenko, I will note for you that this order, as we see in the first paragraph, goes to the Military Districts, the navy, the air force, the air defence. But as can you see, General, it is the number that is listed in General Gotovina's orders. Now, based on your military experience, General, is this the actual -- the chain of what were you talking about during your testimony earlier, that an order comes out at the Main Staff and goes down to a lower subordinate level and then goes down to a more subordinate level. Is that how it generally flows?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And it also goes -- as you see, it gets narrower in scope as it goes down, because this is a multi-service order effective the 25th, and then obviously it goes on down as -- as you see, in -- in the subsequent levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we will offer 1D2948 into evidence 1D2948 into evidence, which is General Cervenko's order of the 25th of August. And then 1D2947, which is General Gotovina's order of 29th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D2947 becomes Exhibit D1639. And 1D2948 becomes Exhibit D1640.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1639 and D1640 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, just one last question before the break. You were shown some documents by counsel during cross-examination and I have shown you some as well that you hadn't seen previously. Has anything happened during cross-examination or since you took the stand here yesterday that caused you to change your opinions with respect to any of the actions taken by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But what I do see is -- on this issue of unity of command, these orders now, as we've gone through the course we see a maturing professional force and the effectiveness of the command. Now you have got commands and orders that could come out very readily out of the main support staff and be disseminated all the way down to the lowest level. It appears that the level of normalcy within the military is starting to build, so that was -- that could be good news and the results of a lot of hard work by a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, General, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is the news, what is good about the news?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The good news is now you're starting to create unity of command all the way -- because if you remember, Your Honour, we started forming this army and we didn't even have doctrine back in 1992. Now you see a maturation of the orders process of the command and control and a doctrine develop and on how you operate as a professional force, and that is probably, to me, evident in the ability now as they're starting to take control of their own destiny, and it appears that the orders process follows fairly smoothly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You consider the copying of orders, addressing them to lower subordinates, as a major development during the month of August 1995, which is an indication of maturing of the professional organisation. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My interpretation is that the sequence of which this happened and the substance of these where each command at each level is re-emphasising and you've got unity of substance in each of these orders going down, I did not see the smooth flow when I first started looking at this. And it seems like we had a little bit as -- as the army was maturing, a little bit of probably additional work to be done in a communications aspect with the unity of command and maturing of the doctrine of which now people understand how to -- how to disseminate and to follow orders. And this to me, if the results of what happened right here reduced ineffective actions by the units, that's a good thing for a military trying to go develop, and that was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This part of your answer, introducing quite a lot of new elements in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because what you were talking about was seeing orders which almost verbatim are repeated lower down the line. Now you earlier told us that you had received some 30 documents to review for your expert opinion. Now did you ever investigate, well, let's say, mid-July or early August, whether similar production of almost verbatim orders down the line happened or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any. I saw the mission -- the continuity of the mission, as you started the offensive OPs from main support staff down to General Gotovina and his dissemination of that order, you know, at least down to his commanders, that it was in the operational perspective. Now see a different facet here of really a fairly smooth although, albeit a reiteration of the same words, that the flow of communications being very much a lot quicker and a lot more understood, that they understood what was going and they passed that information quite readily. The test would be what happened after these orders were disseminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you earlier testified that the delay of seven days in passing an order through down the line was not what you considered to be a timely way of dealing with such a matter. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in your last answer, you expressed your -- your views on professionality of what happened late August. Now the delay you earlier talked I think was mid-August, was 12th to 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, th to 19th, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many documents did you study to analyse what is at the basis of your conclusion? Apart from the ones shown to you in court, did you analyse any other series of issues which were dealt with in orders which then passed down the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not analyse the orders for time and sequential type of analysis and how that communication flowed. I analysed the orders in the past of what they said, what the task organisation and what the mission was given. That was my focus as we got ready to do the operational campaign. I just noted, having watched this sequence here, based on what the counsel have provided and, Your Honour, you just brought up the delay of -- of 12 or one week before the subordinate commander reiterated the importance of protecting the equipment and so forth, and indisciplined behaviour. Here is a case when in a matter of four days you have gone from the highest level of the Croatian authorities all the way down to the operations group very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this demonstrates the growth in professionality in that one week time? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it shows a growth and an understanding and an increase in the communications in the flow unity of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me put to you an alternative interpretation of this and see whether -- do the same exercise we have done before. Let's -- I'm not saying it is my assumption, but for argument's sake, let's say that avoiding devastation of -- or burning and looting was not of a primary concern and therefore everyone took its time; whereas, saving military facilities for future use would be a high priority, and therefore no one would take his time. That is, well, a -- I'm not saying it is the explanation. I don't know. But it is at least a potential explanation, that is, the difference of subject between 12 to 19 August or between the 20th and the 30th of August. Is there any method by which you could establish whether your interpretation would be better than the one - perhaps one out of many - would be -- that your interpretation would be the better one and the more valid one? I'm now thinking in terms of methods and logic of drawing conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you have to look at each of these incidents in a different way, because it's a little bit of apples and oranges. Your first instance where you want to take control and establish the authority into the re-captured free Croatian land, you want the civil authorities to step up and enforce the rule of law. Now, that goes through in the responsibilities to minister of the interior and Mr. -- and the civilian and military police. Normally when things go through a civilian type of organisation, and no offence to anyone here, it maybe here, they are not organised to disseminate and/or do things that quickly. Now, the other perspective that you saw in this order's process is to make sure that when what was previously military infrastructure now becomes cleared and secured for future use. So it's a little bit different where you talk about the control and authority throughout the land and re-establishing that civil authority and this piece where he's talking about protecting particularly the military infrastructure so you can regain the use of it later. It appears to me that -- that this latter part is talking specifically on military infrastructure that had been occupied by another force because they talk about in clearing the area previously occupied, make sure you clear the area from mines, booby traps or any demolition. So that would also be -- that's one paragraph in there, I think, is very important to catch because, if when somebody vacated a military facility they would try to render it unusable to future occupancy, it should be cleared. So I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Aren't you at this moment strongly supporting what I suggested as a possible explanation, that the subject matter may be an important element in how quickly orders were passed down the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Subject matter, yes, sir. And level of importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, the growth of professionalism which was your previous explanation for the difference between mid-August and end August might be competing with difference in subject matter as an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could. It could. It's my observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now we will have a break. We managed to, Mr. Jones, to schedule our hearings today in such a way that you will be able to travel, which means that we'll have one other session which will start at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll adjourn until 3.00. --- Lunch break taken at 1.54 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, you will now be examined by Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for planning purposes, I think I will be considerably less than 30 minutes. I know Your Honours have questions for the witness too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General Jones, I have a few questions for you and at the outset what I wanted to say to you is I'm not actually interested specifically in your opinions, I'm more interested in -- the information you based your opinions upon. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying, just to reiterate where we left off at the end of the last session, you were not asked by the Gotovina Defence team to analyse Mr. Cermak's role in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were not provided with any documents that were signed or drafted by Mr. Cermak, were you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it would be right to say, to emphasise, I think, what you, yourself said, you do you not know anything about the tasks that he performed because you didn't see, I think, what you called his task organisation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see his -- what he was tasked with or his task organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm also right in saying that have you not seen any documents signed by Mr. Cermak addressed to HV units which, you know from your research, were under the command of General Gotovina within the Split Military District; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I don't remember any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now you, yourself, said quite early on in your evidence, and this is actually at page 33, line 25, that a commander can only have responsibility and oversights for units assigned to him. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to a part of your evidence where you were referring to the subordination of the military police and the civilian police. And I'll read it back carefully to you what you said. And this is at page 19, lines 21 to 23. And you said the following: "It appeared to me in the subsequent -- with the meeting with the minister it is said that the military police and civilian police would then work under the minister of the interior and subordinate to him." Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's true. I think the minister of the interior is correct. I may be wrong, but just the military and civilian police would work subordinate to whoever was responsible for restoring the constitutional authority of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you there. Now, I'm not going to produce exhibits because the Judges have already seen them, but I can inform you, I don't think there is any dispute about this fact in the case is that the military police -- there is no evidence at all to show that the military police were subordinated to the minister of the interior in this case. Do you accept that you could be wrong on that point?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the minister of the interior, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That the military police --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You accept that are you wrong on that point. Do you know the name of the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No matter. It doesn't matter. Now, on page 20 at lines 22 to 23, His Honour Judge Orie was asking you a number of questions, and he said to you, "I did not ask you to list them but to say how much approximately," and here he was talking about units that were subordinated to Mr. Cermak. Okay? That's the reference point. Than's at again page 20, line -- lines 22 to 23. And you said: "I would say that he had the military police and the civilian police that would move through the area that was following the operation. My estimate is that there would be three to 500 people." Now, first of all, in terms of the numbers, I'm right in saying that you have seen absolutely no operational orders, reports, or other documents showing that General Cermak had three to 500 people subordinated to him, have you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was referring to Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So that was incorrect, wasn't it, too?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm also right in saying that you have not seen any operational orders or documents or reports demonstrating that Mr. Cermak had operational command of the military police or civilian police. You haven't seen any documents to that effect either, have you, General?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I would like to ask you a few questions, again, on the genesis of your report. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that you were approached by the Defence, that you discussed whether you would be the right person for the job they had in mind, whether you had the experience needed to do that job, and then that you were assigned with the task to prepare the reports. Now, you also told us that you received some documents from the Gotovina Defence. Can you tell us how did you receive them and when did you receive them?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, the sequence went like this: I was contacted by them. I had to work with my company to see that I did not have a conflict of interest. Subsequent to that, then I was given the letter, I think you saw, of May 20th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I then proposed to them an outline, what I thought that they wanted me to talk about. And we agreed that the scope of the paper -- at that time then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did present an outline on the basis of the 20th of May letter or ...

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I did was handwrite an outline and ask them if this is, in fact, the scope of what you were looking for, in terms of my military experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that outline, could you give us some more details, how many pages approximately?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was approximately two pages handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at that moment you had not yet received the documents you were -- you would use for the report.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's correct. I was trying to get the scope of the paper and what exactly the areas they wanted me to address, as I understood their tasking memo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically outlined the logic I would use to write the paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say -- when you received the 20th of May letter, you had already the list of facts, attachment A to that letter, on which -- on the basis of which you would work.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry? The lists that were attached to the letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20th of May letter.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, had the attachment with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, providing the facts.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you had that --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was provided with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you had no documents yet.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then what then happened next.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed with them the scope of the letter, then they provided me documentation to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's take it again step by step. So you sent them the outline.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually I met with them and discussed it with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You discussed it with them.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I showed it to them and how I was going to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember how long that conversation took and where it took place?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was where?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we met in, I believe, Washington DC when I was there for other business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you discussed the outline with members of the team. One member, more members?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, two members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two members. Now, then you -- at that moment, did you receive the documentation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Subsequent to that, they mailed them to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, had you asked for specific documents or was it their selection that they provided to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a combination of things which were germane to the case, the documentation and things additionally I asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the first selection?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first selection was exactly that, it was a combination I asked to make sure I had the orders, the task organisation, the background, and they provided that for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you asked for a specific type of document and they provided you with those types of documents.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: They also provided a few extra documents which supported the outline I had given for me to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you started drafting or did you first ask for more documentation.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- the next thing I did was read and do the research, and then I -- I re-wrote my outline, and then once I was satisfied with the logic of which I was going to address the questions of the 20 May letter, I sat down and wrote the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said the next thing you did was to read and do the research.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the research went beyond reading the documentation that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what did you -- beyond what was provided to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other thing I did was go back in my own documentation, the things I had from my military service and my time in Bosnia and look at such things as the maps I had and exactly where things were. I also went back to my military documents and US doctrine on specific things and looked at the concept of an operational commander and commander's responsibilities. Those were things I personally had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, not knowing what you were actually provided with, do we find all the sources you used in either the report or the footnotes or is there material which cannot be traced on the basis of your report and the footnotes?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that is footnoted was documents provided, or reference out of documents provided. Things that were my opinion and my assessment were largely my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's try to -- you make now a distinction between documents provided to you and opinion and assessment. Now there seems to be a third category, that is documents not being provided to you but in your possession or at least available to you. Do we find anywhere in the report or in its footnotes those documents or that information which was not provided to you by the Gotovina Defence but which you had available, as you said, notes, maps, [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not specific reference in my report to any of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. So we can't verify those sources. Have you listed them anywhere for yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because when I reviewed them like one was FM 3.0 US Army military doctrine or operations doctrine. There was nothing specific enough in there that I would use in my report after I went back and reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you read this material. You did additional research on the basis of what was available to you, of which we do not know exactly what it is. Then you said you started drafting. Did you, at that point in time, or at an earlier point in time or at a later point in time ask for additional documents to the Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a later point in time, after I thought through, I -- what I had written, I asked for additional information. That's where it came into being the issue on numbers of non-combatants in the area. Those kind of questions as I was trying to formulate in my mind exactly what was happening. I also was provided some of the additional testimonies as counsel had spoken to about people who had already testified about non-combatants in the area and how they controlled those, and I just looked at those. I didn't use them in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said you asked for additional information when you thought through what you had written. A draft report, therefore, was already in existence when you asked for this additional information?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had the draft in my computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this additional information, did you send a letter asking for it or how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I verbally asked for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Verbally. Was that in a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was on the phone. And then you received that additional information how?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: They sent me the document and/or passed me -- or told me the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer to what?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relative number of, for example, non-combatants that were in the area. Another question I asked was the law when -- Law of Land Warfare synonymous with the rule of law, or principles of Geneva Convention. Those are some of the clarification questions I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll try to understand. You said another question you asked was the Law on Land Warfare synonymous with the rule of law, or principles of the Geneva Convention. It is not entirely clear to me what question you specifically asked.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me what questions I asked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a question I asked. Because if you remember when they were trying to create their doctrine and their training base back in 1992, 1993, 1994, period I saw where the Law of Land Warfare was referred to as being taught or at least criteria had been taught. So in my experiences, the rule of law, Geneva Convention, are very similar, and I wanted to know what that term was used synonymous with the US doctrinal term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it about how they used it or were you interested in whether the Law on Land warfare was synonymous or was the same as the --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Law on Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to understand basically if they attempted to treat people how to take care of civilians and non-combatants when they were structuring their training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you got an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The answer was: It is synonymous with what the US doctrine considers handling non-combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you asked for some additional information.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You got this information. Then you finalised your draft or what was the next step.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next question I had for them was what was the format for the paper such that you could reference it quickly because I had provided a paper like this before and then they gave me an example of another paper submitted and so I followed that format. I re-did my paper and then as I was waiting to review it once again for myself, then obviously it needed to be submitted. And I provided it so they could get it to the Court in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and not any draft had been submitted at any earlier stage. It was only the final draft that you submitted to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was reiterated that the work would be mine, and I think if you see my paper, I don't think that someone could have -- else could have written that other than a person who had my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not exactly an answer. I was not asking whether someone else had written it. But I asked you whether that was the first time that a draft, apart from the outline of two pages you had discussed with them at an earlier stage, whether there was any draft in between through the two pages outlined and the final version you sent to the Gotovina Defence which was sent to them or available to them.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had -- the answer to your question is: I provided them the final paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And no intermediate version of it.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than discussing the format. I did not provide him -- I discussed a format with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said you were provided with testimony of other witnesses. At what occasion was this done and how was it done?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was provided the -- I was mailed the actual copy of the testimony, so I could review what that person had testified, for my information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember testimony of how many witnesses you received?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I think, two. One was the British officer had experience in peacekeeping. Another was the attache to Croatia at the time, I believe a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you provided with these testimonies in their entirety or a selection of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was provided the court narrative, I believe, the document of what was testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what we call the transcript of --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what you see on your screen, if that is the verbatim ...

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't quite in this format, but I'm sure it was pretty close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was a verbatim report of the testimony of those --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier you would have heard that Mr. Kehoe told us that portions were read to you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Portions of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of -- of other evidence --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- from what I understood, Mr. Kehoe, whether I would have to check that you were referring to the transcript of testimony of Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One of them was Theunens, Judge, and I just need to clarify with regard to some of the statistics that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment -- let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They were also in the facts as given in Appendix A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's ... you were referring to the transcript of Theunens' testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So Mr. Kehoe told us that a selection of the transcript was read to you, whereas you tell us that you received the testimony in transcript format. Now, I was -- I asked you when this was read to you, but you have not confirmed that, Portions of this material were read to me.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, sir, we're talking about two different testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm talking about at this moment is what was, as Mr. Kehoe told us, what was read to you -- Is that -- Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the course of the discussions last weekend, and we got into the discipline, I went back to the transcript and said that the Prosecutor's expert said 151 per cent and that's the page that I gave to you. And that happened in our discussions over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He had the other letter at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then I would have expected the witness to tell us that the only time anything was read to him was last weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Judge, I said that earlier ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will check the transcript in this respect. One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 118, Judge, line 8. During the course of the discussions last weekend, and the transcript, I said to him that 151 per cent, and that -- I was giving you the reference thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was referring to page 63, Mr. Kehoe, where you told us that, for transparency purposes, you had read portions of the testimony of Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I referred to Mr. Misetic's question and Mr. Theunens' answer in the context of the discussion of what kind of disciplinary proceedings were going on, and that was just in the course of a discussion over the weekend while we were going through this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it was not clear to me in what circumstances any portion of the evidence was read to the witness. I asked him that. That's the only thing I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I understand, judge, well, I mean, you understand the circumstance of it at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it was unclear at that moment whether it was when he was still preparing his report or whether it was at any other moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- So you -- let me try to get back to where we were. You had asked for additional documents. Now, the total of approximately 30 documents would that include the additional documents you asked for or would they be in addition to that, and, if so, how many there were, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30 documents should -- should include everything to include one document being the excerpts from the Balkans report the CIA had. I consider that one document although quite large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you drafted the report. There was no further feedback, and that's the report that we received.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drafted a report and submitted it. And I told them I would like to have a chance to elaborate further because obviously I thought I could do more. However, given the time, I said, That should answer the questions you gave me. Can you submit that, if that is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, apparently during briefing, additional information was provided to you. And for the Chamber, it's important to know what information you exactly had. Could you briefly describe what additional information was given to you in whatever form, orally or in writing, at a later stage, after you had given the report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only additional documents I received was a series of three or four documents which were further clarifying orders of subordinates. I can't reference -- they're in this book. I have seen them. And that was in the preparation I asked for. I have never been here, and I asked for a session with the counsel, their representatives to tell me what goes on in the court, and they provided that information so I wouldn't be surprised when I got here. Now, subsequent to that, I did not bring documents with me, obviously. I did bring my paper and this weekend, we talked and that's where the counsel was telling me -- he read me some things in answering my questions. That's the preparation I went through to -- there's nothing I used as reference -- the information here that I don't think that is not already admitted in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. A final topic I would briefly deal with. Were you ever informed about discussions in which the political leadership would take part? I'm talking about the political leadership of Croatia, in which the demographic situation, perhaps the desired demographic situation, as far as the presence of Serbs in the Krajina area was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only information I have on that, Your Honour, is the orders initially put out which was to re-claim the -- the internationally recognised territory of Croatia by defeating the RSK which was the enemy force considered at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what would be, apart from the military objectives, what may have been objectives or not objectives of some matters not to be desired is how many Croats, how many Serbs would finally populate that area was -- have you any knowledge about any such discussions in which the political leadership was involved?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I, therefore, take it that awareness of Mr. Gotovina of such discussions, or presence during such discussions, that you have no information about that either?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not seen anything on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Jones, you may have noticed from my last question that I was referring to Mr. Gotovina. I addressed you as Mr. Jones during your presence here in court. This has got nothing to do with disrespect for ranks or titles. It is my habit to address whoever comes to this court, unless there's a specific reason to do otherwise, just by mister. I hope you will understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem, sir, I can appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Mr. Waespi, any further questions for the witness? Have the questions of the Bench triggered any need to put further questions to the witness? Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can discuss a matter outside the presence of the witness given the fact that he speaks English, but I will tell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is any matter which should be appropriately addressed in the absence of the witness, Mr. Jones, you are the victim, because it's easier to ask you to leave the courtroom than for all of us to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Judge, when I answered this question and do it by asking a question with going back, Judge, to the basis of Your Honour's questions, in a sense of, was he privy to any conversation or go through any conversation where the political leadership talked about the level of Serbs. I mean, is Your Honour talking about a specific meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we -- first of all, this Chamber received evidence and don't ask me to summarise all of it, but that matters were discussed, for example, I remember that -- I think it was a discussion that Mr. Galbraith said something about it, about whether or not one wished Serbs who would have left to return, and I remember percentages were used there. I think as a matter of fact, but again I'm just seeking information, I know there are some sources. If my recollection is right, that -- that it appeared in one way or another in the Brioni meeting as well. But I hope you're not testing my accurate knowledge at this moment of where exactly to find it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there is in the evidence, there are a few -- there are a few instances where these matters do appear, and I just wanted to know whether this witness was, again, whether he was privy to any such information, whether right or wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that, at least we can assess whether such information would have had any impact on forming an opinion about a lot of matters, and I'm fully aware that the opinions are not primarily about these kind of matters. At the same time, the witness gave a rather broad opinion about the performance of Mr. Gotovina, especially at the end of his testimony in-chief, there was a rather broad appreciation of -- of how Mr. Gotovina had performed. And I was seeking to -- to find out what kind - just as I did before on documentary evidence - what kind of information may have played a role in forming an opinion because it may not come as a surprise but portions of the sources he apparently has consulted are in a grey area for the Chamber at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question was actually more specific in trying to be as responsive as I can to the Chamber and not on my client, but primarily as an officer of the court is, you know, the question concerning a political meeting or -- that General Gotovina was present at, I mean, the frame of reference of what political leadership meeting was General Gotovina at, and that's -- that's the source of my dilemma in -- and the reason why, in the main, I raise to my feet because I'm somewhat perplexed by that question by the Chamber. Because I have no -- no such political leadership meeting that my client attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just asking the witness whether he knows anything about it, yes or no. And since his sources are unclear, I put it in a very open way, and I was talking about awareness, for example, of such -- I put it would say specifically in a rather broad perspective and context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any reason to -- for further questions to the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Then we could ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, it appears that there are no further questions for you, which means that we have concluded your -- concluded hearing your evidence in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, and I wish you a safe trip home again, and I'm glad that we were able to accommodate you as far as your travelling schedule was concerned. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I trust that I have helped. Good look to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we had this additional session just to finish the testimony of Mr. Jones, there's no reason, I think, to continue and ask whether the next witness is ready. I take it that the next witness will be called tomorrow. There's one small procedural issue I would like to deal with; that is, a decision in relation to the statement of Mr. Sterc, the 92 ter statement of Mr. Sterc, and more specifically on the heading of paragraph 5 of his statement. The Chamber would like to correct on the record its ruling in relation to the 92 ter statement of Witness Sterc, which states on transcript pages 20343 to 20344 that the heading of paragraph 5 of his statement was not admitted into evidence. The Chamber noted that, in the version of the statement that has now been uploaded in e-court, the heading of paragraph 5 has remained, and the Chamber is of the view this need not to be taken out. The version of the statement as now uploaded in e-court can thus remain unchanged and the heading of paragraph 5 is admitted into evidence, as part of the portion of the statement that is admitted into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. Is there any procedural issue to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to the issue yesterday concerning the, quote/unquote, 92 bis witnesses, Mr. Russo and I have communicated. It's my understanding that the Prosecution may go into other matters that are not directly related to the immediate substance of the witness statements. So we would ask that we be allowed to proof for two reasons; one is that, in essence, these are now 92 ter statements, and so I believe, and I'm sure the Chamber will correct me if I am wrong, that I will have to take the witnesses through the 92 ter attestations prior to admission of the statements into evidence so, to that extent, there may be -- there may be changes in the statements. I don't know that unless I am able to communicate with them or corrections to the statements. Second is, again, I believe we're entitled to try and test the credibility of our own witnesses, and I will tell the Court that I have no intention of - and I've told Mr. Russo this - leading any evidence that is not already in the statement. However, I would just like to proof them just for my own knowledge concerning credibility. But there will be no additional testimony other than what's in the witness statements themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just one point, Mr. President. I didn't mean to communicate to Mr. Misetic that we would be going into matters not directly covered by the witness statements. That's not to say that we may not present evidence or put questions to the witness in order to test the credibility of the assertions they make in their witness statements. So this is a bit of a border-line issue. I'm not sure where the line is to be drawn. Of course, we don't take a position on whether or not the Defence should be permitted to proof the witnesses. That's for the Chamber to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, did you intend to go through the statements or did you also intend to give an opportunity to the witness to read the statement of the witness which apparently contradicts the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to meet the -- meet or communicate with them so they could review their own statements, make any corrections, changes, that needs to be made so that the 92 ter attestation can be made under oath. If there are any changes, I will send a supplemental information sheet around, otherwise I will take them through the 92 ter process and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your intention just is to ask them whether there are any corrections to be made --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and whether -- just to prepare the attestation rather than to inform the witness about possible contradictions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- Mr. Russo, under those circumstances, do you have any objections if Mr. Misetic would be allowed, for this limited purposes, to proof the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, Mr. President, we do have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, within the limits you explained to the Court, set out to us, you may proof the 92 bis/then 92 ter witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other procedural matter? If not, then we'll adjourn and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 2nd of September, quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
